en: The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume One, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Great Forest at Vaiśālī, preaching from a multi-storied pavilion.
The Buddha was dwelling in the hall together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, during the early morning, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, put on his robes and took up his bowl to enter the city for alms. Having returned to his lodging, finished his meal, and washed his face and hands, he put away his robes and bowl and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Bring me my sitting mat; I shall now go to the Cāpāla Caitya to enter meditative concentration and contemplate."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went to that place together with Ānanda.
Upon arriving there, Ānanda spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), whereupon the World-Honored One sat cross-legged and remained in silent contemplation.
At that time, Ānanda was not far from the Buddha; he too sat upright in meditation in another place.
After a short while, the World-Honored One arose from his concentration and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In this Vaiśālī, there are the Udāyana Caitya, the Gautama Caitya, the Āmra Caitya, the Bahuputra Caitya, the Sāla Caitya, and the Capala Caitya. These caityas are most delightful."

Ānanda! If those who possess the four bases of psychic power can still remain for the full duration of an eon, or slightly less than an eon, how could the Tathāgata, who now possesses great supernormal power, be unable to remain for an eon, or slightly less than an eon?
At that time, although the World-Honored One had thus opened the door for such a request by speaking these words to Ānanda, Ānanda remained silent and did not realize it.

Even when the World-Honored One spoke with earnestness three times, Ānanda was utterly bewildered and still failed to understand, failing to entreat the Tathāgata to remain for an eon, or even slightly less than an eon, for the benefit of the world’s devas and people.
Why is this? It is because he has been deluded by the Māra King.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words three times; yet seeing that Ānanda’s mind was still not awakened, he remained silent.
At that time, Māra came to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is now the proper time for you to enter parinirvāṇa; Sugata!"
It is now appropriate for me to enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
In the past, when I was by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, I entreated the World-Honored One to enter parinirvāṇa, and at that time the World-Honored One replied to me:

"My fourfold assembly—of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—is not yet complete, nor have I yet subdued the various other non-Buddhists; therefore, it is not yet time for me to enter parinirvāṇa."

“World-Honored One, now the fourfold assembly is fully complete, and you have already subdued all other non-Buddhists; all that was to be accomplished has been finished. It is now time for you to enter parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the Māra made this request three times, and the Tathāgata immediately replied: "Excellent!
In the past, by the side of the Nairañjanā River, I already granted you my word; however, because the fourfold assembly was not yet complete, it has remained so until now."
"Now that they are fully perfected, in three months' time he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, the Māra-king leaped for joy and returned to his celestial palace.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately relinquished his life-span, yet through his supernormal powers he sustained his life for three months.
At that moment, the great earth shook with eighteen signs, celestial drums resounded of their own accord, and by the power of the Buddha, a voice proclaimed from the sky:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
When the assembly of devas and humans suddenly heard this sound, their hearts were filled with great sorrow and distress, and blood appeared all over their bodies.
At that moment, the World-Honored One spoke these verses at that place:
"All sentient beings Are subject to birth and death."
"I am now likewise subject to birth and death, yet I do not follow after existence;
all conditioned activities, I now wish to relinquish.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One remained silent.
At that time, Ānanda saw the great earth tremble; his heart was filled with great alarm and fear, and he thought to himself:
"For what reason has this phenomenon suddenly appeared?"
"Such a matter is no small cause; I shall now go to consult the World-Honored One.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!"

As I was contemplating elsewhere, facing toward him, I suddenly saw the great earth tremble in eighteen ways and heard the sound of celestial drums in the sky; my heart was filled with great terror, for I did not know what the causes and conditions of these signs were.
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! There are eight causes and conditions for the great earthquake:

First, the great earth rests upon water; this vast water rests upon the wind-circle; and this wind-circle rests upon space. At times, when fierce winds arise in space and blow against that wind-circle, the wind-circle moves, and as the wind-circle moves, the water moves; and as the water moves, the great earth shakes.
Second, when bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have cultivated supernatural powers first achieve them, they cause the great earth to shake in order to test their own attainments.
Third, when a Bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven is about to descend and enter his mother’s womb, he causes the great earth to shake.
Fourth, when the Bodhisattva was first born, emerging from the right side [of his mother], the great earth shook;
fifth, when the Bodhisattva left the royal palace, went forth to study the Way, and attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the great earth shook;
sixth, when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment and began to turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma for the sake of humans and devas, the great earth shook.
Seventh, when the Tathāgata relinquishes his lifespan, he remains by sustaining his life through the power of supernormal knowledge;
therefore, the great earth shakes. Eighth, when the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, the great earth shakes.
Ānanda! You should know that there are these eight causes and conditions for the shaking of the earth. Ānanda!

There are eight classes of beings: first, the kṣatriyas; second, the brāhmaṇas; third, the elders and householders; fourth, the śramaṇas; fifth, the Four Heavenly Kings; sixth, the Trāyastriṃśa devas; seventh, the Māra kings; and eighth, the Brahmā kings. Regarding these eight classes of beings, I observe their faculties and, for those who are ready to be delivered, manifest various forms according to their needs and preach the Dharma to them; yet they do not know that it is I who am speaking.

Ānanda! There are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): first, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are limited in scope; second, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are immeasurable in scope; third, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are limited in scope; fourth, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are immeasurable in scope; fifth, one perceives all forms as blue; sixth, one perceives all forms as yellow; seventh, one perceives all forms as red; eighth, one perceives all forms as white. These are the supreme and superior dharmas for the practitioner.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are eight liberations: first, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; second, not having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms while contemplating their impurity; third, the liberation of the beautiful; fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the liberation of the attainment of cessation. These, too, are the superior dharmas of the practitioner.
"If one can thoroughly master these dharmas, one will attain sovereign mastery and unimpededness regarding all dharmas.
Ānanda, do you understand?"
In the past, when I first attained the Way, I converted Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa on the banks of the Nairañjanā River.
At that time, Māra came to where I was and addressed me, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Now it is time for you to enter parinirvāṇa, Sugata!
Now it is time for you to enter parinirvāṇa!"
"Why is this? Those who were to be delivered have all attained liberation; now is precisely the time for my parinirvāṇa.
Thus he requested three times, and I replied:
"This is not yet the time for my parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because my fourfold assembly is not yet complete, and those who are to be delivered have not all reached their ultimate goal."
"The various assemblies of non-Buddhists have not yet been subdued.
Having received these three answers, the Māra King, his heart filled with grief and distress, immediately returned to his celestial palace.
Just now he came again and requested me, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is now appropriate for you to enter parinirvāṇa."
"Sugata! It is now appropriate for you to enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this so?"
In the past, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, I entreated the World-Honored One to enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, the World-Honored One replied to me, saying:

"My fourfold assembly—of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—is not yet fully perfected; furthermore, I have not yet subdued the various other non-Buddhists. For these reasons, it is not yet appropriate for me to enter parinirvāṇa."
“World-Honored One!
Now the fourfold assembly is complete, and all other heterodox teachers have been subdued; what was to be done has been entirely accomplished. It is now fitting that you enter parinirvāṇa.”
When the Māra-king had thus made his request three times, I replied:
"In the past, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, I already granted you my word; however, because the fourfold assembly was not yet complete, that is why it has remained until now."
"Now that I have fully perfected [the path], in three months' time I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
When the Māra King heard these words of mine, he leaped for joy and returned to his celestial palace.
"Having received this invitation from Māra, I immediately relinquished my life-span and remained for three months; it is because of these causes and conditions that the great earth shook.
At that time, Ānanda, hearing these words of the Buddha, was overcome with great sorrow; his blood appeared all over his body, and weeping with streaming tears, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"Out of compassion for us, may you remain for a kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, to benefit the world’s devas and human beings.
Thus he requested three times.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"It is not the time for you now to request the Tathāgata. Why is this?
I have already granted the Māra that three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"Why do you now request that I remain?
Ānanda, since you have attended me, have you ever heard me speak two different words?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"Indeed, I have never heard that the Teacher of Gods and Men has spoken with double meanings.

In the past, I have heard the World-Honored One preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, saying: 'A person who possesses the four bases of psychic power can remain for the duration of a kalpa, or even less than a kalpa. How much more so for the Tathāgata, the sovereign king of immeasurable spiritual powers!"
Now we can no longer remain for a kalpa or even slightly less than a kalpa; instead, we shall relinquish our life-span and remain for only three months.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will have compassion for us and remain for a kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa!
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Ānanda:
"The reason I now relinquish my life-span is precisely because of you. Why is this so?"
I previously said to you here:

"If those who possess the four bases of spiritual power can still remain for the full duration of a kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, how much more so the Tathāgata, who now possesses great supernormal powers—could he not remain for a kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa?"

"Thus, even after I had spoken these words with such earnestness three times, opening the door of exhortation and request, you remained silent and never asked me to remain for an eon, or even slightly less than an eon."
"Therefore, I shall now remain for three months; how can you now request that I remain?

At that time, Ānanda, hearing these words from the Buddha, knew with certainty that the Buddha was entering parinirvāṇa and could not be entreated to stay. His heart was filled with agony; he fainted in grief and distress, his tears flowing incessantly as he could not restrain himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that Ānanda was overcome with great anguish and distress, comforted him with his Brahma-voice, saying: "Ānanda!
You should not now give rise to sorrow or grief. Such is the nature of all conditioned phenomena: everything that comes together must inevitably part."
The World-Honored One then spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena Ultimately return to impermanence;
Those joined by affection and love Must inevitably part."
"All conditioned phenomena are thus; one should not give rise to sorrow or distress.
Thereupon, Ānanda shed tears and said, "The Teacher of gods and humans, the Unsurpassed Great Honored One, will before long enter parinirvāṇa; how could I now not feel sorrow and distress?"
He immediately struck his head and cried out in a loud voice: "Alas!
How bitter!"
"The Eye of the World has perished!
Before long, sentient beings will lose their compassionate father!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"You should not now give rise to grief and distress; even if one were to remain for a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, one must eventually perish. Such is the nature and characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma); do not harbor suffering toward me alone."
"I now wish to return to the multi-storied lecture hall; you may take my sitting mat for me.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, returned to the multi-storied lecture hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and tell all the bhikṣus in this great grove, at the multi-storied lecture hall, to proceed together to the Great Assembly Hall."
Ānanda, having received the command, immediately addressed the entire assembly of bhikṣus: "The World-Honored One commands that you all proceed to the Mahāsannipāta Hall.
Once the bhikṣus had assembled, Ānanda informed the Buddha:
"The assembly of bhikṣus has all gathered."
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will know the proper time himself.
At that time, the Tathāgata went from the multi-storied lecture hall to the Great Assembly Hall, where he spread out his seat and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus:
“The various dharmas I have previously taught for you, reflect upon them constantly; recite and practice them without neglect.”
Purify your holy life and uphold the prohibitive precepts, bringing benefit and welfare to the world’s devas and human beings. O bhikṣus!
Whatever Dharma I have previously taught for you, contemplate it and do not give rise to indolence.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—should be cultivated by you with diligent application and reflection; these dharmas can lead one to the state of liberation.
Furthermore, monks, all phenomena are entirely impermanent; body and life are fragile and precarious like a flash of lightning. You should not give way to negligence.
"You should all know that before long, after three months have passed, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I wish to cast off this Decayed and aged body."
Now that I have relinquished my life-span, I remain with only three months left.
Those who were to be transformed and delivered have all been brought to completion;
therefore, it will not be long before I enter parinirvāṇa.
The various dharmas I have taught are your teachers;
receive them upon the crown of your heads and guard them with care. Practice them without neglect or forgetfulness;
through diligent and earnest effort, you shall be no different from me.
Birth and death are extremely precarious; body and life are entirely impermanent.
Constantly seek liberation and do not engage in heedless conduct.
With right mindfulness and pure contemplation, skillfully guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts.
With a concentrated mind and focused contemplation, one restrains the emotions from external objects.
One who can act in this way protects the True Dharma,
personally attains the state of liberation, and benefits all devas and humans.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, their hearts were filled with great anguish; tears flowed profusely, blood appeared all over their bodies, and overcome by confusion and distress, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will remain in this world!
Do not enter parinirvāṇa!
Benefit all sentient beings and cause the realms of humans and devas to flourish.
I only pray that you will remain in this world!
Do not enter parinirvāṇa!
Open the eye of wisdom for all sentient beings.
All sentient beings have fallen into darkness; we pray only that the Tathāgata will act as a luminous illumination for them!
All sentient beings are adrift and submerged in the great ocean of birth and death; we pray only that the Tathāgata will act as a vessel for them!
Raising his hands, he struck his head, beat his breast, and cried out:
"Alas! How bitter it is!"
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa; upon whom shall all sentient beings rely?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All dharmas are entirely impermanent; where there is a union through affection, there is no separation that does not follow."
You should not request that I remain in the world.
Why is this? Now is not the time to exhort me; I have already briefly taught you the essentials of the Dharma, which you should uphold well, no different from how I do.
As the day drew to a close, the World-Honored One returned with Ānanda to the multi-storied lecture hall.
Then, when the following morning arrived, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city with Ānanda to beg for food.
Having obtained food, he immediately returned to the multi-storied lecture hall; after finishing his meal and rinsing his mouth, he went with the bhikṣus to the village of Khaṇḍa.
While traveling through the city of Vaiśālī, the World-Honored One turned his gaze toward the city and smiled.
Ānanda immediately prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and asked the Buddha:
“O Unsurpassed Great Honored One!”
"It is not without cause or condition that one laughs falsely.
The Buddha then replied, "Ānanda!"
"The reason I smiled while heading toward the city just now was precisely because this would be my final sight of this city.
When the Tathāgata spoke these words, rain fell from the sky without any clouds.
Thereupon Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is truly extraordinary!”
"The void is pure and free from any mist or obscuration, yet suddenly such a dense rain has fallen.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you understand this?"
The devas in the void, hearing my words that this was the final sight of the city of Vaiśālī, were deeply distressed; moved by grief, they wept, and these were the tears of the devas, not rain.
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard these words of the Buddha, were again overcome with grief and distress; they fell to the ground in a swoon and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, O Devamanuṣya, you are in the midst of extreme suffering; why does the World-Honored One wish to abandon us and enter parinirvāṇa?"
At that time, the Tathāgata comforted them with a Brahma-voice, saying:
"You should not give rise to sorrow or suffering.
The bhikṣus said:
“The World-Honored One now views Vaiśālī for the last time; before long, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. How could we not be filled with grief and suffering!”
Thus it was passed from person to person, word spreading until it reached the ears of all the Licchavis.

Upon hearing these words, the Licchavis were overcome with grief and distress; their bodies turned the color of blood, and they raised their hands to strike their heads, beating their breasts and crying out loudly: "Alas!"
"Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished; now sentient beings have no refuge.
Thus they spoke to one another.
"We should now go to the Buddha's presence and entreat the World-Honored One to remain in Vaiśālī for a kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, to bring benefit to the world’s devas and human beings."

He immediately prepared his carriage and hastened to the Buddha’s dwelling. Having exited the city gate, he beheld the Tathāgata from afar, as well as Ānanda and the various bhikṣus, who were weeping profusely and overcome with grief and distress. The Licchavis, seeing this, were all the more moved by sorrow and lamentation. They proceeded to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you are now about to enter parinirvāṇa. All sentient beings will lose the eye of wisdom and find themselves in the midst of darkness; how then shall they be able to see the path they ought to travel?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain for a kalpa, or at least for slightly less than a kalpa.
Thus he requested three times.
The Buddha then replied:
"All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent; even if they should endure for an eon or slightly less than an eon, they ultimately return to impermanence.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Though Mount Sumeru is high and vast, It will ultimately be worn away and consumed."
Though the great ocean is deep and vast, it too shall eventually dry up;
though the sun and moon are bright and clear, they do not long remain before setting in the west;
though the great earth is firm and solid, it can bear the weight of all things.
When the kalpa ends, the fires of karma burn, and all likewise return to impermanence;
those joined by love and affection must inevitably part.
Even the Tathāgatas of the past, with their indestructible vajra bodies, [have passed away].
They too are subject to impermanent change; how could I alone be different?
Such is the nature of all Buddhas’ teachings;
you should not entreat me, nor harbor further grief and affliction by being partial toward me.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavis:
"Cease your weeping; listen attentively to what the Tathāgata has finally declared."
The Licchavis said: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"We wish to hear it with joy.
Thereupon the Tathāgata spread out his sitting mat and sat down cross-legged; the assembly of bhikṣus and the Licchavis, restraining themselves with great effort, each sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavis, saying:
"You should know that there are seven kinds of dharmas which increase day by day and do not diminish."
First, they are joyful and harmonious, without any mutual opposition;
second, they mutually enlighten one another and discuss virtuous deeds;
third, they protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts as well as the rules of decorum.
Fourth, to revere one's parents and other elders;
fifth, for relatives to live in harmony, each showing deference and compliance to the others;
sixth, to repair and make offerings at the caityas within the realm.
Seventh is to uphold the Buddha-dharma, to personally honor and respect bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and to cherish and protect upāsakas and upāsikās.
If these seven dharmas are received and practiced, they will cause a person’s majesty and virtue to increase daily, the state to flourish, and the people to enjoy abundance and happiness.
"From this day forth until the end of your lives, you should uphold these [precepts] and must not be indolent.
At that time, the Licchavis addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If we were to practice even a single one of these seven dharmas, it would still cause our majesty and virtue to increase; how much more so if we practice all seven dharmas in their entirety!"
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We have now attained benefit and merit; we shall uphold this for as long as we live, never forgetting it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you too should cultivate the practice of seven dharmas.
The first is to be joyful and harmonious, like water and milk."
Second, they constantly assemble together to discuss and expound upon the sutras and the Dharma;
third, they uphold the prohibitive precepts without giving rise to thoughts of transgression;
fourth, they show reverence toward their teachers and those of seniority.
Fifth, to provide for the needs of forest-dwelling bhikṣus with love and respect;
sixth, to exhort and convert donors to construct and maintain dwellings for the Three Jewels;
and seventh, to apply oneself with diligent vigor to protect the Buddha-Dharma.
"You should know this: if a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas, his merit and wisdom will increase day by day.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!"
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas that you should cultivate:
first, do not engage in the worldly occupations for acquiring a livelihood as laypeople do;
second, do not engage in frivolous discourse or mocking speech.
Third, not delighting in sleep and neglecting diligent effort;
fourth, not discussing worldly matters that are without benefit;
fifth, distancing oneself from evil associates and drawing near to virtuous friends.
Sixth is right mindfulness, which does not give rise to perverse thoughts;
seventh is that if one has attained anything within the Buddha-dharma, one seeks further advancement.
If you all can practice these seven dharmas, your merit and wisdom will increase day by day.
"Furthermore, monks! There are seven further qualities that you should practice.
First, generate firm faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
Second, possessing a sense of shame;
third, possessing a sense of dread of blame;
fourth, the mind always delighting in extensive learning.
Fifth, the mind is not flighty or restless;
sixth, one delights in hearing the meaning of the sūtras;
seventh, one delights in cultivating wisdom.
"If you are able to cultivate these seven dharmas, your merit and wisdom will increase day by day.
Furthermore, monks! There are further seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) which you should practice."

First is the discernment of dharmas, second is diligence, third is joy, fourth is mindfulness, fifth is concentration, sixth is tranquility, and seventh is equanimity. If you are able to practice these seven dharmas, your merit and wisdom will increase day by day.
"Furthermore, monks! There are seven other dharmas. First, contemplation of impermanence;

second, contemplation of non-self; third, contemplation of impurity; fourth, contemplation of suffering; fifth, lack of delight in the world; sixth, non-attachment to the five desires; seventh, diligent cultivation of cessation. If you are able to practice these seven dharmas, your merit and wisdom will increase day by day."
"Furthermore, monks!
There are seven other qualities that you should practice.
The first is to constantly practice loving-kindness with the body."
Second, one constantly practices loving-kindness through speech;
third, one constantly practices loving-kindness through the mind;
fourth, if there are donors who provide various kinds of alms, one distributes them equally among all without allowing for partiality.
Fifth, one delights in preaching the profound and sublime Dharma without weariness;
sixth, one does not instruct others using worldly treatises;
seventh, upon seeing those who are not fellow students, one does not give rise to hatred or envy.
"If you are able to cultivate these seven dharmas, your merit and wisdom will increase day by day.
Furthermore, monks!
There are seven more dharmas that you should practice."
First, they are well able to discern the ninefold division of the Dharma;
second, they skillfully understand its meaning;
third, they practice the path and recite the teachings, all at the appropriate times.
Fourth, in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one should skillfully maintain proper decorum;
fifth, when preaching the Dharma to others, one should exercise self-reflection and teach people according to one's own strengths;
sixth, if Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, elders, or householders come desiring to hear the Dharma, one should carefully deliberate and preach in accordance with their spiritual capacities.
Seventh, skillfully distinguish between the foolish and the wise.
If you can practice these seven dharmas, your merit and wisdom will increase day by day, and you will be able to protect my True Dharma.

At that time, the Licchavi wives of the kingdom, hearing that the Buddha would soon enter parinirvāṇa and that this was their final sight of Vaiśālī, were deeply distressed and wept with lingering sorrow. Each, accompanied by five hundred attendants, prepared five hundred chariots laden with offerings and various ornaments. Those drawn by white oxen hung white banners and canopies; likewise, those of other colors—such as black or yellow—each followed the color of their oxen. They departed the city one after another and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw them approaching from afar and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see these Licchavi women coming, leading and following one another, so exceedingly magnificent and beautiful?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“The deportment of this Licchavi elder of Vaiśālī and his wife, as they enter and exit, is so magnificent and refined that it is no different from that of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.”

At that time, the Licchavi wife, having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated herself with her head at his feet. She wept piteously and was so overcome with grief that she could not compose herself; she then made offerings to the Buddha with various ritual implements and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will remain in this world to teach and transform sentient beings.
World-Honored One, if you were now to enter parinirvāṇa, we would be left blind and dark, never again attaining awakening.

Having received birth with meager merit, we possess these female bodies; we are constantly subject to limitations and lack autonomy, and thus have no opportunity to draw near to the World-Honored One frequently.
“If the World-Honored One intends to enter parinirvāṇa, our roots of goodness will daily diminish.
At that time, the Tathāgata replied to them, saying:

“From this day forth until the end of your lives, you must diligently uphold the precepts as a person protects their eyes; keep your thoughts upright and honest, and do not give rise to flattery or envy. This itself is how you shall always see me.”
When the Licchavi wives heard these words of the Buddha, their grief intensified manifold; unable to restrain themselves, they withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the daughter of Āmra was of such exquisite countenance that her beauty was unsurpassed in the world.

Hearing that the Buddha would soon enter parinirvāṇa and that he was to be seen for the last time in the city of Vaiśālī, his heart was filled with grief and distress; tears flowed freely as he immediately set out from the city with five hundred attendants, preparing five hundred chariots, proceeding in succession to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, World-Honored One!
Seeing her approaching from afar, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“The daughter Ambāḷā is now coming to visit me; her appearance is exceptionally exquisite, peerless in all the world. You should all maintain an upright mind and right mindfulness, and do not give rise to attachment.”
"Monks! You should contemplate this body as containing various impurities: the liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys, feces, urine, pus, and blood fill its interior."
Within it dwell eighty thousand families of worms;
hair, fur, nails, and teeth cover the thin skin over the flesh, from which the nine orifices constantly flow—therein is not a single thing to be found pleasant.
Furthermore, this body, from its very origin, arises from impurity.

Every place where this body goes or comes becomes drenched in filth; though it may be adorned with carvings and colors and perfumed with famous incenses, it is like a precious vase containing foul excrement.

Furthermore, at the time of death, the body becomes bloated and putrid, its joints and limbs are severed, and worms within the body devour it; moreover, it is swallowed and consumed by tigers, wolves, owls, hawks, eagles, and vultures.
The people of the world are deluded and unable to observe correctly; they are attached to affection and love, clinging to them until death, and give rise to craving within these circumstances.
How could any wise person take pleasure in this?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Though one may wear necklaces and adorn oneself with fragrant flowers, Within lies impurity:
excrement, urine, saliva, and mucus."
Sentient beings cherish and cling to it, Deluded and failing to awaken;
It is like fire covered by ashes, Upon which the foolish tread.
The wise should keep far away from it, And never give rise to a mind of defiled attachment.

At that time, the woman Āmrapālī approached the Buddha, prostrated with her head at his feet, and made offerings to the Buddha with various ritual implements. With tears choking her voice, she spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
May you remain in this world for the duration of your lifespan and not enter parinirvāṇa, so as to benefit the devas and people of the world!
If the World-Honored One were to definitely enter parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings would have no further guide, like infants who have lost their compassionate mother.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying:
"The nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are thus; you should not now give rise to grief or distress."
The World-Honored One then spoke the Dharma for the sake of the entire assembly that had gathered, saying:
"From this day forward, you must uphold the prohibitive precepts and not allow them to be violated.
Those who break the precepts are detested and loathed by devas, nāgas, and spirits alike!"
A foul reputation spreads abroad, and people take no pleasure in seeing him; if he is among a multitude, he alone lacks majestic virtue.
The various benevolent spirits and deities no longer provide protection.

At the time of death, when the mind and consciousness are filled with terror, even if one possesses even the slightest merit, one will not remember it at all. Immediately upon dying, one will undergo the sufferings of hell according to one's karma, remaining there for the duration of kalpas before finally emerging. Thereafter, one will again take the form of a hungry ghost or an animal; thus revolving from state to state, there is no prospect of liberation.
A bhikṣu who upholds the precepts is revered by devas, nāgas, and spirits alike.
His excellent reputation spreads abroad, reaching throughout the world.
Amidst the great assembly, his majestic virtue is radiant and flourishing.
"Various benevolent spirits and deities will constantly follow and protect them.
At the time of death, their right mindfulness will be clear and distinct, and immediately upon dying, they shall be reborn in a pure realm.

When the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma, sixty-eight thousand nayutas of devas and humans from the eight classes of beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Sixty bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and their minds liberated, became arhats.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavis, their wives, and Āmrapālī:
"I now wish to proceed to the village of Khaṇḍa; you may each return to your respective dwellings."
"You should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent; you should simply practice the Dharma I have taught, and do not weep or lament like infants.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat.

At that time, the Licchavis, along with their wives and the daughter of Āmrapālī, having heard these words of the Buddha, beat their breasts and struck their heads, wailing and crying out loudly; they followed the Buddha along the road, refusing to turn back.

Seeing that their longing and attachment were so profound that they could not be consoled by mere words, the World-Honored One immediately employed his supernormal powers to manifest a river with steep, inaccessible banks and a torrential current.

At that time, the Licchavis and their retinues, along with the lady Āmrapālī, having seen the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus on the riverbank, were overcome with redoubled grief and distress; they fell prostrate upon the ground in a swoon and, in faint voices, spoke to one another:
"How is it that this great river has suddenly appeared here, and moreover, why are its waves and currents so turbulent and swift?"
"This must have been done by the Tathāgata because he saw that we were following him and would not leave him; he did this merely to sever our path!

At that time, the Licchavis, along with their wives and the Āmrapālī, having failed to attain deliverance, felt their hearts leap with even greater intensity; bowing their heads and sobbing, they returned home in despair.
At that time, the Tathāgata went to the forest north of the village of Khaṇḍa and stayed there. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that there are four dharmas: first, ethical discipline; second, meditative concentration;
third, wisdom; and fourth, liberation. If one does not hear of or know these four dharmas, such a person will remain for a long night in the ocean of birth and death."
"In the past, had I not heard and known these four dharmas, I would not have been able to quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation— Had I not heard of them for long,..."
One cannot swiftly realize the unsurpassed, true, and right path.
You all should apply yourselves with diligence and cultivate these four dharmas;
you will be able to sever the suffering of birth and death and become the supreme field of merit for devas and humans.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One analyzed and explained in detail the meaning of these four dharmas for the bhikṣus.
While the Tathāgata was preaching this Dharma, one thousand two hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind regarding all phenomena, becoming arhats.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, rose from his seat and proceeded toward Hastigrāma, Āmragrāma, Jambugrāma, and so on, until he arrived at the city of Sāketa.
Having arrived at that city, surrounded by the bhikṣus in front and behind, he sat down in a certain place.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four noble truths; you should diligently observe them."
First is the truth of suffering, second is the truth of the origin [of suffering], third is the truth of cessation, and fourth is the truth of the path.
Monks, as for the truth of suffering, it refers to the so-called eight kinds of suffering:

first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death; fifth, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; sixth, the suffering of association with the disliked; seventh, the suffering of separation from the beloved; and eighth, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
You should know that these eight kinds of suffering, as well as all phenomena subject to outflows (*āsrava*), are truly suffering in reality because they are oppressive.
As for the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serve as the causal basis for these eight sufferings.
One should know that this Truth of Origination is the cause of suffering.
As for the Truth of Cessation, it is the cessation of ignorance and craving, which cuts off the cause of suffering.
One should know that this Truth of Cessation is indeed cessation.
The Truth of the Path consists of the Eightfold Noble Path:
first, right view; second, right mindfulness; third, right intention; fourth, right action; fifth, right effort; sixth, right speech; seventh, right livelihood; and eighth, right concentration.
These eight factors constitute the Noble Path.
If one applies oneself with diligence and contemplates these four dharmas, one will swiftly depart from birth and death and reach the state of liberation.
"O bhikṣus, if among you there are those who have reached the ultimate consummation in this Dharma, you should also diligently explain it for the sake of others.
After my parinirvāṇa, you should likewise apply yourselves with diligence to reflection and practice."
When the Tathāgata had spoken this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and their minds liberated, became arhats.
Forty thousand devas from the heavens, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement regarding all dharmas, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four definitive declarations.
First, if there is a bhikṣu who desires to preach the Dharma, he speaks as follows:”
"I have personally heard such a teaching from the Buddha; I have well understood its meaning, received and upheld it, recited it, and attained complete mastery of it.

You should request him to explain it, and according to what you hear, you should carefully reflect upon it: "Is this found within the Sūtras, or is it within the Vinaya, or among the characteristics of the Dharma?"
If this teaching is found within the Sūtras and the Vinaya, according to their respective characteristics, it should be accepted and upheld, and one should praise it as excellent.

If this teaching is not found within the Sūtras and the Vinaya, according to their respective characteristics, it should not be accepted or upheld, nor should it be praised; one should know that this teaching was not spoken by me.
Second, if there is a bhikṣu who desires to preach the Dharma and says:
"In such-and-such a place, among a community of bhikṣus, I heard this Dharma; I have well understood its meaning, and I have received, upheld, recited, and mastered it with complete proficiency."

"You all should request him to speak; having heard the Dharma, you must carefully reflect upon it for yourselves: is this a Sūtra, is this Vinaya, or is this the Abhidharma? Does such a teaching exist?"
If this Dharma exists within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma (Dharmalakṣaṇa), it should be received and upheld; one should praise it, saying, "Excellent!"
If this teaching is not found within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the characteristics of the Dharma, it should not be accepted or upheld, nor should it be praised.
One should know that this teaching was not spoken by me, nor was it spoken by that assembly of bhikṣus.
Third, if there is a bhikṣu who desires to preach the Dharma, he speaks thus:

"I personally heard this Dharma from a certain elder bhikṣu at such-and-such a monastery or such-and-such a forest hermitage; those many elder bhikṣus were all widely learned, intelligent, and wise. Having heard this Dharma, they well understood its meaning, received and upheld it, recited it, and attained complete mastery of it."

"You should all request him to explain it; then, according to what you have heard, you should reflect upon it well: Is this a Sūtra? Is it Vinaya? Or is this teaching found within the Dharma-lakṣaṇa?"
If this Dharma is found within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma (Dharmalakṣaṇa), it should be received and upheld; one should praise it, saying, "Excellent!"
If this teaching is not found within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the characteristics of the Dharma, it should not be accepted or upheld, nor should it be praised.
One should know that this teaching was not spoken by me.
Fourth, if there is a bhikṣu who desires to preach the Dharma and speaks as follows:

"I personally heard from a certain elder bhikṣu—wise and of great learning—who resides in a certain monastery or forest hermitage, that he has heard such a Dharma, well understands its meaning, and has received, upheld, recited, and mastered it with complete proficiency."
"You all should request him to speak; once you have heard it, you should reflect upon it well: Is this a Sūtra? Is it Vinaya? Or is this teaching found within the Dharma-lakṣaṇa?"
If this Dharma is found within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the characteristics of the Dharma (dharmalakṣaṇa), it should be accepted and upheld; one should praise it, saying, "Excellent!
If this Dharma is not found within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the characteristics of the Dharma, it should not be accepted or upheld, nor should it be praised.
You should know that this teaching is not spoken by me; you should properly discern these four definitive teachings, and furthermore, transmit these discerned teachings to others.
"Whether I am in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa, you shall know the false from the true by this.
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha,
saying, "Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, we shall be able to distinguish between what the Buddha has spoken and what Māra has spoken.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat with the bhikṣus and proceeded toward the village of Kośala.
Having arrived at that village, he sat beneath a tree, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him.

At that time, the brahmins, elders, and householders of that village, having heard that the Buddha had arrived, all hurried and vied with one another to come to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Why have you now come to this village with the bhikṣus, having a different destination?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata replied to him:
"Three months from now, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Departing from the city of Vaiśālī, I have traveled through various villages and towns, arriving here in due course."

At that time, when the people heard these words of the Buddha, they wept with grief and distress, fell to the ground in a swoon, raised their hands to strike their heads, beat their breasts, and cried out loudly, saying: "Alas!"
"Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished; before long, we shall lose our guide and refuge.
Shedding tears, they spoke thus.
“May the World-Honored One, we pray,
remain for the duration of one kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to them, saying:
"You should not give rise to such grief and distress. Why is this?
Such is the nature and characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
You should set aside your feelings of sorrow and distress, and listen with a tranquil mind to my final teaching."
Thereupon, those people forcibly restrained themselves, lowering their heads and listening in silence.
At that time, there was among the assembly a brahmin named Vāgīśa, who was clever, wise, widely learned, and possessed of a powerful memory.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed them, saying:
"You should know that there are four dharmas which those living as householders ought to cultivate."
First, to revere one's parents, serving and supporting them with all one's heart;
second, to constantly instruct and guide one's wife and children with wholesome dharmas;
third, to take pity on servants and laborers, taking note of their needs and circumstances.
Fourth, associate with virtuous friends and distance yourself from evil persons.
If you all constantly practice these four dharmas, you will be loved and respected by others in the present life, and in future births, you will always dwell in auspicious places.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are four unwholesome dharmas for a householder.
First, he does not repay the wealth of others and shows no sense of shame or remorse;

second, he possesses immense and vast riches which he begrudges and does not spend, providing nothing for his parents, wife, children, kinsmen, or relatives, nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.

Third, he is exceedingly wealthy and possesses vast riches; he wears magnificent clothing, indulges his palate with the finest flavors, provides for his parents, and bestows gifts upon all his relatives and kinsmen; he serves śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
fourth, his actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely free from evil; he is intelligent and wise, and delights in extensive learning.
"You should know that although householders may possess these four kinds of happiness, being free from debt to others and free from stinginess and greed is called the lowest form of happiness;
being fond of practicing generosity is called middling happiness;

and when one’s actions of body, speech, and mind do not commit evil, and one possesses intelligence and wisdom while delighting in extensive learning, this is called the most excellent form of happiness."
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Being free from debt and stinginess is called the lowest happiness;
possessing wealth and practicing generosity is called middling happiness."
Purity of body, speech, and mental action; wisdom and delight in much learning—this is the supreme bliss, the practice of the wise.
From this day forth, until the end of your lives, you must [abide by this].
"Let the old and the young instruct one another, practicing this middle and superior Dharma.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Volume Upper;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Volume Middle.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
At that time, Pāpabhūti and others addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!
From this day forward, we shall mutually instruct and guide one another through the middle and superior dharmas.”
Thereupon, Upavartana and his five hundred followers immediately received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts in the presence of the Buddha.
Upavartana and the others addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept our offerings tomorrow."
At that time, the Tathāgata granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had consented, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and the others rose from their seats and, together with the assembly that had come with them, paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
Returning to his house, he prepared fragrant and delicious food and drink throughout the entire night. When the next day arrived and the time for the meal was approaching, he sent a messenger to say:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will..."
"Know for yourself that the time has come.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, went to his house and sat down in due order.
When Upavartana saw that the Buddha and the Sangha were all comfortably seated, he rose and went to serve water, personally offering various exquisite foods and drinks.
Five hundred other brahmins, elders, and householders, each carrying fine delicacies, were also present in the house, together making offerings to the Buddha.

At that time, among the bhikṣus at the meal, there were those who did not properly maintain their bodily deportment; when the brahmins, elders, and householders saw this, they were not pleased in their hearts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the assembly, addressed them all, saying:

"You should know that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is as profound and vast as the ocean, beyond measure. Furthermore, within the great ocean there are sentient beings whose bodies are extremely large—some ten thousand six thousand yojanas in height, some eight thousand yojanas, some four thousand yojanas, some one thousand yojanas, or even one inch or half an inch, down to the size of an atom. The ocean of the Tathāgata’s Dharma is likewise so."

Among them, there are some who have attained arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges (*traividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), possessing great majesty, virtue, and the merit of devas and humans;

among them are also those who have attained the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), as well as those who are candidates for the four fruits, even including ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet obtained the benefits of the Dharma.
Therefore, you must not give rise to a mind of obstruction within this ocean of Dharma.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"As all the flowing rivers Ultimately return to the great ocean,
So too does the merit from offering food To the Buddha and the Sangha return to oneself."
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he further preached various teachings for the multitude.
Thereupon, the five hundred people, including Pāpabhūti and others, became free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat with the community of bhikṣus and proceeded further forward toward the city of Pāpā.
The five hundred people, including Upavartana, wailed and wept as they saw off the Tathāgata; they lingered and gazed longingly until their hopes were extinguished, and only then did they return.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had arrived at that city, there was a son of an artisan named Cunda; he possessed a garden that was exceedingly secluded and tranquil.
The Tathāgata, surrounded by the bhikṣus preceding and following him, went and stayed in that garden.

At that time, when Cunda heard that the Buddha and the Saṃgha had arrived at his garden, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; together with his companions, he went to where the Buddha was.
He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, then stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wonder, World-Honored One!
For what reason have you come here?”
"Is there another destination?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to him, saying:
"The reason I have come here now is that before long I shall enter parinirvāṇa; for this reason I have come, so that we may see one another for the last time."
At that time, Cunda and his companions, hearing these words of the Buddha, were overcome with great sorrow and fainted upon the ground. After a long while, they spoke to the Buddha in a low voice:
"World-Honored One, do you now abandon all sentient beings and no longer regard them with compassion?"
Why do you wish to enter parinirvāṇa so soon?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will remain for the duration of a kalpa!
"If it were to be reduced by one kalpa!
He then struck his head with his hand, beat his breast, and cried out loudly, saying:
"Alas! Alas!"
Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished!
From this day forward, all sentient beings shall sink into the ocean of birth and death, with no time of emergence in sight.
"Why is this? Because the Unsurpassed Guide has entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
“You should not now give rise to suffering and distress.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) are like this; they are all subject to the transformations of impermanence (*anitya*). Where there is the gathering of affection and love, there must inevitably be separation.”
"Therefore, do not give rise to grief or distress now.
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I too now know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; those who meet through affection and love must all eventually part."
"Yet the Unsurpassed Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa; how could I not be grieved and distressed?
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately preached various teachings for Cunda.
Having heard this, Cunda’s grief subsided slightly; he rose from his seat, adjusted his physical deportment, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One, I only pray that you will accept my humble offering tomorrow.”
The World-Honored One then granted his consent by remaining silent.
At that time, Cunda, knowing that the Buddha had consented, prostrated at his feet and withdrew. Cunda returned to his home and prepared many kinds of exquisite food throughout the entire night.
When the time for the morning meal arrived, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"May the World-Honored One know that it is time."
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the bhikṣus in front and behind, proceeded to his house and took his seat in due order.
At that time, Cunda, seeing that the Buddha was seated, immediately served water and, with his own hands, portioned out and presented various exquisite delicacies.
When the World-Honored One and the Saṃgha had finished eating and washed their bowls, they returned to their original seats, and Cunda also sat down.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
"You have now performed a rare merit by providing the final meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; such a karmic fruit as this shall never come to an end."
Among all sentient beings, there is none whose accumulated merit can equal yours.
You should give rise to a heart of joy and celebration; for I have now finally accepted your invitation and shall no longer accept further offerings of food from others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"You have now established rare and wondrous merit;
In your final life, you shall obtain a meal offering For the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
Your merit increases daily, never reaching exhaustion.
You should now give rise to a heart of profound joy;
among all who have performed meritorious deeds, none can equal you.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"I am now suffering from physical pain and wish to go quickly to the city of Kuśinagara."

At that time, Ānanda, together with the bhikṣus and Cunda, having heard these words of the Buddha, were overcome with great anguish; they wailed and lamented incessantly, unable to restrain themselves.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and, surrounded by the bhikṣus preceding and following him, proceeded toward that city.
At that time, Cunda also followed the Tathāgata with his retinue. On the way, the World-Honored One stopped beneath a tree and said to Ānanda:
"I am currently suffering greatly from abdominal pain."
He then took Ānanda and, not far from the tree, blood began to flow from him.
Having returned beneath the tree, he instructed Ānanda:
"You should take my saṃghāṭī robe, fold it four times, and spread it upon the ground; I wish to sit and rest, for I am no longer able to proceed further."
Ānanda received the command, and the World-Honored One immediately sat down to rest beneath a tree. He then addressed Ānanda again:
"I am now afflicted by thirst; you should go to the Kakutthā River and fetch some pure water."
Ānanda replied, "Just now there were merchants with five hundred wagons passing by the river; the water must have become turbid, and I fear it will not be fit for drinking."
Thus he commanded Ānanda a second and a third time, and only then did Ānanda take his bowl and depart.
Upon reaching the riverbank, he saw that the water was perfectly clear; his heart was filled with great terror and the hair on his body stood on end as he thought to himself:

"Just now I saw five hundred merchant wagons pass through this water, yet it remained turbid. I did not realize it would suddenly become so clear, which has caused me to repeatedly disobey the Tathāgata’s command."
He immediately took the water back and offered it as a service, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!

Previously, I saw five hundred merchant carriages crossing the river, which obstructed the flow before and behind; even after ten days, the water should not yet have been clear. Yet by the World-Honored One’s supernormal power, in the space of a mere moment, it has become limpid and pure."
The World-Honored One then accepted the water and drank it.
At that time, there was a son of a seer named Pūrṇa, called Vakkali, who was a disciple of that seer Kāla.

From Kauśāmbī, he proceeded toward the city of Pāpā; suddenly, along the way, he saw the Tathāgata sitting at rest beneath a tree. He joined his palms in greeting, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As for the dharma of leaving the household life, the practice of sitting meditation is foremost. One must subdue the sensory faculties so that the mind is not distracted, remaining single-mindedly focused and tranquil, beyond the reach of alarm or fear."

Why is this? I recall that in the past, while following my teacher, the seer Kālāma, as we were traveling along a road, we became weary and exhausted. We drew near to the side of the path and rested beneath a tree; my teacher then immediately sat in meditation and entered contemplation.

At that time, there were several merchants passing by from the front, traveling in fifty wagons; my teacher at that moment remained silent as before, his body unmoving, and it was only after a long while that he arose from meditation.
I immediately went and said to my teacher:

"Venerable Sir, while you were sitting in meditation just now, there were merchants with fifty wagons passing by in front of you; their noise was like the roar of thunder. I wonder, did you see them or not?"
The teacher replied to me, saying,
"I saw nothing at all.
I asked him again:
"Did you hear its sound? He replied, "I did not."
He then spoke again, saying:
"The reason there is this dust and dirt staining your robe, Venerable One, is simply because that vehicle passed by.
At that time, I felt a profound sense of wonder and knew that the practice of sitting meditation is most worthy of reverence.
"By skillfully restraining the faculties of the senses, none are able to cause distraction.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pukkasa:
"What you have just said is nothing extraordinary."

Why is this? If there were a person who was neither in deep sleep nor entered into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), yet sat upright in meditation, and five hundred chariots passed before them, and this person at that time neither perceived nor heard them—only then could such a thing be called marvelous.

Furthermore, Vakkali, this is not yet to be considered a great marvel: if there is someone who sits in meditation with right mindfulness and encounters a celestial thunderbolt, lightning, and a dazzling flash of thunder.
At that time, there were two brothers who were plowmen; hearing this, they were struck with terror and died instantly, and four oxen likewise collapsed and perished on the spot;
yet the practitioner of dhyāna remained unaware and did not hear a thing.
"Can this be called extraordinary?

Vakkali replied, "That five hundred chariots passed by before me without my perceiving or hearing them was already extraordinary; how much more so that a thunderbolt, flashing and shaking the earth, could pass without being heard or perceived—this is truly most rare!"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pukkusa:
"In the past, while I was at the village of Acaṇḍa, I sat cross-legged beneath a tree and engaged in contemplation."
At that time, there were five hundred merchant carriages passing by me, yet as I was absorbed in meditative contemplation, I was neither aware of nor heard them.
Only after the merchants had passed for a long while did I emerge from concentration.
At that time, those merchants saw me rising from afar and all came rushing forward. Seeing the dust and dirt upon my body and my soiled robes, they immediately brushed them away and asked me:
"World-Honored One, did you see the five hundred wagons that passed by here just now?"
He then replied,
"I do not see it. He asked again:
“World-Honored One, you may close your eyes and not look; do you still hear sounds?
I answered again:
“I do not hear sounds either.”
The merchant asked again:
"World-Honored One, are you sleeping,
or have you entered the meditative absorption of cessation?"
I replied again:
"I was not sleeping, nor had I entered meditative absorption.
I was simply engaged in contemplation; therefore, I neither heard nor saw."
When those merchants heard these words of mine, they were struck with great wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying:
"The power of meditative concentration can indeed be like this!"
I then taught them various dharmas.
At that time, the entire assembly of merchants, regarding all dharmas, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
"Furthermore, Vakkali!"
In days past, I was sitting alone in a field beside that village, silently engaged in meditative contemplation.
Before long, suddenly a great thunderclap struck from the heavens; lightning, thunder, wind, and rain shook heaven and earth.
At that time, there were two brothers who were plowmen; suddenly hearing this sound, they were both struck with terror and fell as if dead.
Furthermore, four oxen likewise collapsed instantly.

At that time, the villagers, hearing that two plowmen had perished in terror—perhaps their parents, wives, children, or close friends—gathered together from the entire village and followed along, weeping as they came to look.
At that time, I had just awakened from meditation and saw muddy water on the ground, as well as a great multitude of people gathered there wailing and weeping.
A man came forward, and I immediately asked him,
"For what reason have these people gathered here in such sorrowful lamentation?"
That person replied:
"World-Honored One!
Did you not perceive the sound of the thunderclap just now?"

"In my village, two brothers were plowing here when they were both struck and killed by lightning at the same time, and four oxen also died together; how is it that the World-Honored One was unaware of this?"
"Was the Tathāgata just now asleep,
or had he entered the meditative absorption of cessation?
He then replied:
"I was not asleep, nor had I entered meditative absorption; I was sitting in tranquil dhyāna, and therefore I did not hear you.
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, that person felt profound wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, thinking to himself:
"Sitting in dhyāna possesses such power as this!"
“I then preached the Dharma to him in various ways.
Having heard the Dharma, he attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena.
At that time, Vakkali, hearing these words of the Buddha, was struck with wonder and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Previously, when I observed my teacher sitting in meditation, he did not hear or know even as fifty chariots passed by, and I considered that to be extraordinary.
Yet now, the Tathāgata has described these two matters such that they cannot be compared even by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions; the power of the Tathāgata’s dhyāna is inconceivable."
He immediately received the three refuges from the Buddha.

The Tathāgata preached various sublime dharmas for him; having heard the Dharma, his mind was opened and his intellect awakened. He became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
He then said to his attendant: "Take two pieces of my golden *karpāsa* cloth and bring them here; I wish to offer them to the Buddha."
The attendant, having received the command, immediately brought it forth.
At that time, Pukkusa held a *karpāsa* cloth in his hands, knelt before the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"I now offer this to the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and graciously accept it."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pukkusa:
"I shall now accept one sheet for you; you may give the other sheet to Ānanda."
Why is this? Ānanda has attended upon me day and night, and today he is attending to my illness.
If there is a donor who makes offerings to both the sick person and the one who nurses them, this is called the fulfillment of a great gift.

At that time, Vakkali, having heard these words from the Buddha, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately placed one cloth beneath the Buddha’s feet, and taking another, he went to where Ānanda was, knelt down on his right knee, and said:
“I now offer this to the Venerable One; I only pray that you will accept it.”
Ānanda replied: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"Since you are now able to believe the words of the Teacher of Gods and Humans, which shall bring you long-lasting peace and happiness for a great night, I accept you as a disciple.
Thereupon, Vakkali returned to the place where the Buddha was; the Tathāgata then preached the various Dharmas to him once more, and having heard the Dharma, he attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
Then, Vakkali addressed the Buddha once more, saying,
"I now wish to go forth in the Buddha's Dharma.
The Buddha immediately called out to him:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
At these words, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa, attaining the state of an Arhat.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted various kinds of light from the opening of his face—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and crimson.
Thereupon Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wonder, World-Honored One!
What causes and conditions have led you to manifest this auspicious omen?”
The Buddha replied:
"Ānanda, you should know that there are two occasions on which I emit great radiance."
First, when he was about to attain Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree, he emitted a great radiance; second, when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he emitted a great radiance.
Ānanda, do you understand?
When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and enter *parinirvāṇa* at the end of the night, it shall be just the same.

You should know this now: at the end of the final watch of the night, I shall enter *parinirvāṇa* between the twin *śāla* trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River in the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas.
Having spoken these words, the assembly of bhikṣus and the devas in the sky wailed and wept, unable to restrain themselves.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, went to the Kakutsthā River, where the World-Honored One immediately entered the river to bathe.
Having finished bathing, he sat with the community of bhikṣus on the bank of the river.
At that time, Cunda reproached himself, thinking:
"Because the World-Honored One accepted my offering of food, he has suffered from abdominal pain and wishes to enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing Cunda’s thoughts, addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You should now know this: let no sentient being reproach themselves by saying, ‘Because the Tathāgata accepted my offering of food, it caused his body to fall ill and he entered parinirvāṇa.’”
Why is this so? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, there are two kinds of people who obtain the most supreme merit.
The first are those who come to offer gifts at the time when he is about to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Second, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, there was the final offering of food.

The merit of these two individuals is exactly equal and without distinction; the retribution they shall obtain is beyond measure. Such acts of giving as these are difficult to encounter, occurring only at rare intervals like the udumbara flower.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda:

"The thought currently in your mind should not give rise to such remorse and self-reproach. You have already obtained the unsurpassed and most difficult-to-attain treasure; you ought instead to feel a sense of joy and gratitude."
Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, the name of a Buddha is difficult to hear.
Though one may hear the name, it is again difficult to see the Buddha.
Though one may see the Buddha, making offerings to him is yet more difficult.
Although you have received offerings, these two kinds of giving are also extremely rare.
You have now achieved the fruit; before long, you shall obtain eloquence, wisdom, physical strength, and longevity.
At that time, Cunda, hearing these words of the Buddha, felt such overwhelming joy that he could not contain himself, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How wonderful!
World-Honored One!"
"I have now attained such great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The giver obtains merit; The one with a compassionate heart has no enmity."
"The doer of good eliminates evil; one who is free from desire has no affliction.
If one practices such conduct, before long one will attain parinirvāṇa.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he addressed Cunda, saying:
"You should now extensively proclaim for others this merit of your final offering, so that those who hear it may obtain peace throughout the long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to proceed to the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River in Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas."
Ānanda replied: “Indeed,
World-Honored One!”

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the bhikṣus in front and behind, proceeded on his way, crossed the Hiraṇyavatī River, and stayed outside the Śāla grove at the birthplace of the Mallas in Kuśinagara. He addressed Ānanda, saying: "Go to the Śāla grove;

there you will see a pair of twin trees standing alone in one place. Sweep beneath them and make the area pure. Arrange a rope bed with the head toward the north, for my body is now extremely pained and exhausted."
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, hearing these words of the Buddha, were overcome with even greater grief and desolation.

Ānanda shed tears and, having received the command, departed; he went to the foot of that tree, swept and sprinkled it, and prepared the offerings, all according to the Dharma. He then returned and reported:
"The sweeping, sprinkling, and preparation of the offerings have all been completed."

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, entered the Śāla grove and went beneath the twin trees. He lay down on his right side with one foot upon the other, sleeping like a lion, with his mind upright and his mindfulness correct.
At that time, flowers suddenly bloomed on the twin trees and fell upon the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One then asked Ānanda:
"Do you see how those trees have produced flowers out of season as an offering to me?"
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, I see them.

At that time, the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, and spirits—rained down various exquisite flowers from the midst of the sky: *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha. They further scattered fragrances such as ox-head sandalwood and performed celestial music, singing hymns of praise.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see the devas and the eight classes of beings in the void making offerings to me?
Ānanda replied:
“Yes, indeed, I have seen it.
The World-Honored One spoke again to Ānanda, saying:
“One who wishes to make offerings to me and repay my kindness need not necessarily do so with these incense, flowers, and musical performances.”
"To purely uphold the prohibitive precepts, to read and recite the sūtras, and to contemplate the profound and wondrous meaning of all dharmas—this is what is called making offerings to me.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Upamāna, who, before the Tathāgata had yet taken Ānanda as his attendant, used to constantly attend to him and look after his needs.
At that time, when Upamāna saw the Tathāgata lying beneath the twin trees, his heart was filled with great anguish, and he stood before the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One addressed him, saying:
"You need not lean against me now."
Upamāna then stepped aside.
At that time, Ānanda felt a doubt arise in his mind:
"I have served the Buddha for many years, yet I have never before seen the Buddha speak in such a manner."
For what reason today do you not permit me to stand before you?
The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa, yet you still do not permit me to weep before you.
Thereupon Ānanda immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and said:
“World-Honored One!

Since I began attending the Buddha until now, I have frequently stood before the World-Honored One, yet I have never heard you tell me to step back. For what reason do you now command Upamāna to move aside?”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! When the various devas,
nāgas, spirits, and the eight classes of beings hear that I am lying on my right side between the twin śāla trees, they will all come vying with one another to behold me.”
From the void, they accumulated down to the earth, filling the four directions to a depth of thirty-two *yojana*s each.
This Bhikṣu Upamāna stood before me; the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, felt a sense of displeasure and thought:
"The Tathāgata is now between the twin trees and will soon enter parinirvāṇa; at this final moment of our beholding him, this bhikṣu stands before the Buddha."
For these reasons, they were made to turn back.
Do you know, Ānanda?

Among these eight classes of beings now, some weep with grief, unable to restrain themselves; some are distressed and bewildered, on the verge of fainting; some pull out their own hair with their hands; and some tear off their ornaments—yet all of them cry out in unison, saying these words:
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s entry into parinirvāṇa!
