The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter; he appears only occasionally, like the udumbara flower, yet now he will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
Alas! How bitter it is!
The Eye of the World has been extinguished; from this day forward, who shall be our guide and refuge?
The gods who have transcended desire all sighed and said:
"Alas! The world is utterly impermanent!
There is no one who undergoes birth and does not return to extinction."
Furthermore, those devas said to one another:

"In the past, when the World-Honored One was staying in Vaiśālī, or in Rājagṛha, or in Śrāvastī, or in other places, and had completed his summer retreat, the community of bhikṣus would come from the four directions to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health."

"Because of this, we were able to see various bhikṣus by the roadside, pay them homage and make offerings, and listen to and receive their teachings on the Dharma, thereby obtaining long-lasting benefit and merit.
Now that the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, the community of bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat, no longer come to inquire after our welfare."

"In the places where they travel, we shall no longer be able to see the bhikṣus by the roadside to pay them homage, make offerings, and listen to their teachings; from now on, we shall forever lose such blessings and benefits."
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, saying:

“If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to intentionally resolve their minds to go to my four sites, the merit they obtain will be beyond measure. In whatever place they are born, they will always dwell among humans and devas, experiencing the fruits of bliss without end.”
What are these four?
First, the place where the Tathāgata was born while he was a bodhisattva, in the Lumbinī Garden of the kingdom of Kapilavastu;
second, the place in the kingdom of Magadha where I first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Third is the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;
fourth is the place of parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the śāla grove beside the Hiraṇyavatī River in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas—these are the four places.

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as others belonging to the assemblies of non-Buddhist paths, should resolve to go there to pay homage, the merit they obtain shall be entirely as described above.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard these words of the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I shall universally proclaim to the fourfold assembly that they should know these four places; if they go there to pay homage, their merit shall be such as this.”
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are upāsikās with virtuous minds who well maintain the practice of the precepts, who delight in hearing the Dharma, and who wish to see the bhikṣus, how should we, from this day forward, conduct ourselves toward them?”
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, you must not have any further contact with him. Ānanda said:
“If we should happen to encounter them by chance, what should we do?
The Buddha said,
“Do not speak with them.”
Ānanda said: “If they do not converse with him, how should those who wish to request instruction and hear the Dharma proceed?
The Buddha said:
"You should preach the Dharma, but you must properly restrain your body,
speech, and mind. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha,
saying, "From this day forward, we shall practice accordingly."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, after you have entered parinirvāṇa, what shall be the method for making offerings?”
The Buddha said:
"You should not now harbor anxious forebodings over this matter.
Simply reflect for yourself: "
"After my parinirvāṇa, you shall protect and uphold the True Dharma, joyfully preaching to others what you have heard in the past. Why is this?
The devas themselves shall provide offerings to my body."
"Furthermore, brahmins, kings, elders, and householders—these shall themselves provide offerings for my body.
Ānanda said: "Although devas and humans may spontaneously offer such worship, I do not know by what dharma I should rely [in performing it]."
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! The manner of making offerings to my body is based on that of a wheel-turning sage king.”
Ānanda asked again:
"What is the method for making offerings to a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda! As for the method of making offerings to a Wheel-Turning Sage King: one uses fresh, pure cotton and fine silk to wrap his body, layering them up until they reach a thickness of a thousand folds. He is then placed within a golden coffin; next, a silver coffin is made to enclose the golden one; then a copper coffin is made to enclose the silver one; and finally, an iron coffin is made to enclose the copper one.

Afterward, various exquisite fragrant oils are poured over them. Furthermore, inside the coffins, various fragrant flowers are scattered and applied as ointments. Then, various musical instruments are played, and songs and hymns are chanted in praise before the lids are lowered.”
They constructed a great jeweled carriage, making it exceedingly high and wide, adorned with various wonders such as canopies, railings, and balustrades; they placed the coffin upon it.

Furthermore, they prepared a site for cremation within the city, sweeping and sprinkling the four directions until it was perfectly pure, and piled up a great pyre of fine sandalwood and various famous incenses.
Furthermore, upon the pyre, they spread fine silk and cotton cloth and set up a great jeweled canopy to cover it.

Then, having lifted [the bier] and proceeded to the cremation site, they offered incense and scattered flowers, making offerings with music. They circumambulated the fragrant pyre seven times, after which they placed the coffin upon the pyre and doused it with scented oil.
The method for lighting the fire is to start from the bottom.

Once the cremation is completed, the śarīra are collected and placed inside a golden jar; immediately at that spot, a stūpa is erected, adorned with a bannered pillar, and draped with silk streamers, flags, and canopies.
All the people should constantly offer various kinds of worship every day by burning incense and scattering flowers.
Ānanda, you should know that such is the manner of worshipping a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

When my body is cremated, it shall be treated in the same manner as that of the King; however, there is one difference regarding the stupa: its banner-pole should be adorned with nine parasols suspended from it.

If there are sentient beings who hang silk banners and canopies, burn incense and scatter flowers, and light lamps and candles to prostrate before and praise my stūpa, such persons will obtain great benefit and merit throughout the long night; moreover, before long, others will also erect great stūpas for their bodies and make offerings to them.
“Ānanda, you should know that all sentient beings do not possess a *stūpa*; only four types of persons may have a *stūpa* erected for them.

First is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—who out of compassion for sentient beings is worthy of being the supreme field of merit for the world; for him, a *stūpa* should be erected.

Second is the Pratyekabuddha, who awakens to the Path through self-realization by contemplating all phenomena and is likewise able to bring benefit and happiness to the people of the world; for him, a *stūpa* should be erected.”

The third refers to the Arhat, who, having contemplated the Dharma as he heard it, has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*); such a person is also able to bring benefit and merit to the people of the world, and for him a stūpa should be erected.

The fourth refers to the Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin-rāja*), who has planted deep roots of merit in past lives and possesses great majestic power; ruling over the four continents with the seven treasures complete, he personally practices the ten wholesome paths of action and further exhorts the people of the four continents to likewise practice the ten wholesome paths; for him, too, a stūpa should be erected.
Ānanda! You should know that if there are sentient beings who offer various articles of worship to this stūpa, the merit they obtain will vary according to their respective degrees of excellence.
At that time, Ānanda, hearing these words of the Buddha, felt a surge of anguish and wept aloud with lamentation.
He hid behind the Buddha, not far from him, and in a low voice spoke thus:

"I am still but a person on the stage of training; I have not yet attained the profound flavor within all dharmas. Now that the Teacher of Gods and Humans has suddenly abandoned me to enter parinirvāṇa, when shall I tread the path of liberation?"
He immediately raised his hand and grasped a branch of a tree, beating his chest and striking his head, falling into a swoon in bitter distress.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the other bhikṣus:
"Where is Ānanda at this moment?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"Ānanda is currently behind the Tathāgata, beneath a tree, weeping and lamenting in distress.
He further told the bhikṣus:
"You may go there and say to Ānanda:
'The Teacher of gods and humans now wishes to see you.
The bhikṣu then went and delivered the Tathāgata’s message.
Having heard this, Ānanda immediately returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked Ānanda:
"Recently I have already told you that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and that the union of affection and love must inevitably lead to separation."
Why do you still give rise to such grief and distress now?
Furthermore, Ānanda!

"From the distant past until now, you have served me; in attending to my every movement—whether advancing or withdrawing, coming or going—and in receiving guests, you have always acted with propriety and moderation.
Furthermore, I observe that your body, speech, and mind are entirely pure and free from blemish; the merit and blessings you have obtained are beyond measure."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Ānanda should not feel such grief and distress. Why is this? Because:”
Before long, you shall attain the state of liberation.
Monks, you should know that all Buddhas of the past had attendants just as Ānanda has now; all Buddhas of the future will likewise be so.

"Monks, you should know that this Ānanda here possesses profound and subtle wisdom, being intelligent and of sharp faculties; all the Dharma-treasuries I have taught since the past, Ānanda has entirely remembered and retained them without forgetting."
Furthermore, monks, Ānanda well knows the proper timing for approaching or withdrawing. If there is a guest who wishes to come and see me, Ānanda first considers the time:

"The World-Honored One should perhaps see the bhikṣus at such a time; or he should see the bhikṣuṇīs at such a time; or he should see the upāsakas at such a time; or he should see the upāsikās at such a time; or he should see the brahmins at such a time; or he should see the kṣatriyas at such a time; or he should see the elders and householders at such a time; or he should see the various non-Buddhist practitioners at such a time."
"When such a multitude as this comes to see me and hears my preaching of the Dharma, they shall all obtain abundant merit and benefit. Why is this?
Because it is through Ānanda’s mediation that they come to see me, and thus their roots of goodness reach maturity."
"Furthermore, monks, a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses four extraordinary and rare qualities.
First, when a brahmin comes to the presence of the Wheel-Turning Sage King and sees him upon arrival—his countenance upright and his majestic virtue lofty and manifest—he feels joy in his heart;
next, hearing the king’s speech, its tone and words being clear and resonant, he likewise feels joy."
Upon seeing the king, he remained silent and spoke no word, yet his heart was filled with exultation;

when taking leave of the king and returning to his dwelling, he looked back with longing and yearning, feeling despondent at every step, like a person suffering from hunger and thirst who fails to find satiety.
Second, the various minor kṣatriyas;
third, the vaiśyas;
and fourth, the śūdras—it is likewise so for these as well. These are the four extraordinary matters of a wheel-turning sage king.
Ānanda, you should know that there are likewise these four extraordinary matters concerning you.
First, when bhikṣus come from afar wishing to pay their respects to me, they all feel joy upon seeing you first;
they likewise feel delight upon hearing your preaching of the Dharma or seeing your silence.
Having taken their leave and departed, they could not contain themselves, for their deep affection for his virtue was boundless.
Second were the bhikṣuṇīs;
third were the upāsakas.
"The fourth is the upāsikā; she, too, is likewise so.
You should know, Ānanda, that he possesses these four extraordinary qualities.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should not now give rise to such self-inflicted suffering as to say:
'The Teacher of gods and humans is about to enter parinirvāṇa; I shall have no further hope for liberation.'"

Why is this? All the treasuries of the Dharma that I have taught, if you contemplate and uphold them after my parinirvāṇa, and practice with diligent vigor, you shall before long attain liberation for yourselves.
At that time, Ānanda, having received the consolation of the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice, his grief and distress were somewhat relieved, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My mind has now awakened slightly; I wish to make a request, so I pray you will have compassion for me."
The Buddha replied,
“What do you wish to request? Ānanda said:
"This city of Kuśinagara, compared to other great kingdoms, is extremely remote and narrow, and its population is not particularly flourishing.
We only pray that the World-Honored One [will consider this]!"
He traveled to other great kingdoms:
Rājagṛha, Vaiśālī, Śrāvastī, Vārāṇasī, Ayodhyā, Campā, Kauśāmbī, and Takṣaśilā; in these cities, he stayed at their very centers.
The population is flourishing and the land is prosperous and joyful; all possess great faith, wisdom, and intelligence.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will travel to those various cities and enter parinirvāṇa there, extensively benefiting all sentient beings therein.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Ānanda, saying:
"You should not now make such a request of me, saying:
'This city of Kuśinagara is remote and narrow.'"
"Listen attentively, and I shall now speak for you. Ānanda!

In the distant past, there was in this city of Kuśinagara a wheel-turning sage king named Mahāsudarśana, who possessed the seven treasures and had a thousand sons capable of subduing enemies; he governed all his subjects solely through the True Dharma."

At that time, this city was named Kuśinagara; its eastern and western gates were twelve yojanas apart, and its northern and southern gates were eight yojanas apart. The city was surrounded on all four sides by seven concentric walls.

Its innermost layer is composed purely of gold; its second layer is composed purely of white silver; its third layer is composed purely of lapis lazuli; its fourth layer is composed purely of crystal; its fifth layer is composed purely of musaragalva; its sixth layer is composed purely of agate; and its seventh layer is a mixture of various jewels.

The city’s watchtowers and battlements all consist of seven stories; their windows, railings, and balustrades are adorned with the seven precious gems. Suspended above them are nets of various precious bells, each positioned at intervals of exactly one arrow-shot’s distance from the next.
The city has four gates, each with nine layers of enclosures, magnificently adorned and decorated, radiant and beautiful to the eye.
Outside the sevenfold walls, there are moats filled with water; this water is clear and pure, possessing the eight meritorious qualities, and all have stairways made of the seven precious gems.
Various kinds of birds—pheasants, phoenixes, peacocks, wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks—soar, wheel, and dance about, gathering there to call out.
Furthermore, the water is filled with *kumuda* flowers, *utpala* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as well as lotuses of blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated colors.

Furthermore, upon its banks, there were seven rows of jewel trees, each row consisting of a different kind of gem; when a gentle breeze arose and blew against their branches, the twigs and leaves brushed against one another, producing sounds like celestial music.
The city was filled to capacity with its inhabitants; it was peaceful, prosperous, and exceedingly flourishing, possessing all the five sensory pleasures just like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Bright pearls were suspended along the roads, so that for the people walking or staying there, there was originally no distinction between day and night.

In this city there are always ten kinds of sounds: first, the sound of elephants; second, the sound of horses; third, the sound of chariots; fourth, the sound of drums; fifth, the sound of conch shells; sixth, the sound of lutes, harps, and the like; seventh, the sound of singing; eighth, the sound of striking bells and clashing chimes during the holding of great assemblies; ninth, the sound of praising those who maintain the precepts; and tenth, the sound of mutual discourse and discussion on the Dharma.

King Mahāsudassana possessed great majesty and virtue; he was foremost in physical beauty, such that all who beheld him loved and revered him. He enjoyed longevity and happiness, and his body was free from even the slightest ailment.

The king’s nature was compassionate and benevolent; he took pity on all beings just as a loving father cherishes his own children. All the people held the king in affection and respect, regarding him as their father.
“Ānanda! On one occasion, King Mahāsudassana desired to go out to the gardens to wander, observe, and enjoy himself; he arrayed his fourfold army, each consisting of eighty-four thousand units.”
Furthermore, the ladies of the inner palace and the court maids likewise prepared eighty-four thousand chariots, wishing to follow along for sightseeing.
At that time, the king further issued a decree to all the brahmins, elders, and householders within the kingdom, ordering them to accompany him on the excursion.
When the preparations for the procession were complete, the Minister of War entered and addressed the King, saying:
"The fourfold army is ready; may Your Majesty know that the time has come.

Thereupon, the King ascended his white elephant palanquin and, surrounded by Brahmins, elders, householders, ministers, and his retinue, as well as the fourfold army, proceeded to the park. The elephant moved with great speed, as swift as a rushing wind.
At that time, the ministers, brahmins, elders, and householders together admonished the king, saying:
"Great King, you have long remained within the deep inner palace; the people outside have had no opportunity to see you."
"Now that we have gone to the gardens for recreation, the crowds of people are packed along the roadside, all looking up in reverence, desiring to see the Great King.
For this reason, I pray you command the charioteer not to proceed with such haste."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately commanded his charioteer: "Drive slowly.
The people by the roadside gazed upon him at their leisure, like children looking upon their father.
At that time, the king saw that all the streets and alleys were perfectly level.
Furthermore, trees made of the seven precious gems stood in rows, providing dense shade, yet there was no pond water.
He immediately commanded a minister:
"Along both sides of all the roads, construct ponds made of the seven precious substances, with each being separated from the next by one hundred bows.
He further ordered that various kinds of famous flowers be planted, and again issued this command:

"Between each pool, attendants were stationed; to those who came to bathe, they provided fragrant flowers and also offered food and drink, allowing them to take as much as they desired until fully satisfied."
"Provide such offerings without ceasing, day or night.
He further commanded that minister:
"From this day forward, whenever people from the four quarters come to beg for alms, you must grant them whatever they require."

Having arrived at the grove, he strolled, observed, and sported with the brahmins, elders, householders, and other ministers until sunset; yet the radiance of the jewels shone so brightly that it was no different from daytime, and it was only by the absence of shadows that he realized it was night.
At that time, after the King had finished sporting with the assembly of brahmins, elders, householders, and other subjects and citizens, he returned to the palace city.
On another day, the brahmins, elders, householders, and great ministers brought various precious jewels and came together to present them to the King. The King then spoke to them, saying:

"Recently, while I was sporting in the gardens, I commanded a certain official: 'From this day forward, should anyone come to request anything, provide it to them according to their wishes. Such is the extent of my giving."
"What do you mean, that you have instead brought these various jewels to offer to me?
At that time, the king immediately reflected within his mind:
"The reason these people have brought jewels to offer to me is entirely because of the high esteem they hold for me within the kingdom."
"Such matters arise from the poverty of the people.

He then commanded his treasury officials to bring forth all manner of precious gems and requisites for living, place them at the crossroads, beat the bells and strike the drums, and proclaim far and wide:
"Great King Mahāsudassana!..."
"Now I open this treasury of jewels to practice giving; if there is anything you require, come and take it as you wish.
Thus King Heng constantly practiced extensive giving, benefiting sentient beings day and night without ceasing.
At that time, the brahmins, elders, householders, and ministers of the kingdom addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!
The palace where you constantly reside is extremely cramped."
"Whenever we come to inquire after the King's health, our attendants are not permitted entry. We only pray that Your Majesty will expand the grounds to make them wider.
Upon hearing these words, the King gave his silent assent and thought to himself:
"I should now enlarge my dwelling place."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the king’s thought, summoned a son of heaven named Viśvakarman, who was exceedingly skillful and capable of accomplishing anything, and said to him:
"In Jambudvīpa, there is a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Mahāsudarśana."

Now that you wish to further expand the palace city, you may descend to serve as the supervising architect, ensuring that his dwelling is as magnificent and exquisitely adorned as mine, without any difference.
Having received the command, that deva immediately descended; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at Jambudvīpa and stood before the king.
When the king beheld the form and majestic bearing of that devaputra, he knew at once that he was no ordinary being and asked him:
"Who are you, O deity, that you have suddenly descended here?"
The deva immediately replied:
"Great King!
You should know that I am a minister of Śakra, Lord of Devas, named Viśvakarman, and I am extremely skilled in the arts."
"Great King, because Your Majesty desires to expand and broaden your palace, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has sent me down to serve as a supervising architect to assist you.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy.
Then, that devaputra immediately began the construction, expanding the palace city; its four gates were spaced twenty-four yojanas apart from one another, and he erected a hall for the king.
Its height, depth, and breadth were each eight yojanas.

Adorned with the seven treasures, it was as magnificent as the palace of Śakra; the palace contained eighty-four thousand chambers and dwellings, each furnished with couches, curtains, and bedding made of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, for the sake of the king, a Dharma-palace was erected, measuring eight yojanas in height, width, and length, adorned with the seven treasures no differently than before.
On the four sides of the palace, there were trees made of the seven treasures and various famous flowers, planted in rows to provide shade and beauty.
Furthermore, he constructed jeweled ponds whose waters were pure and possessed the eight meritorious qualities.
In the center of the palace, a lion throne was provided, adorned with the seven treasures, exceedingly high and wide, covered by a jeweled canopy from which the seven treasures hung down.

Furthermore, for those coming from the four distant quarters to hear the Dharma, he prepared four kinds of precious thrones—of gold, white silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—numbering eighty-four thousand in total.
Once Viśvakarman had completed the construction of the palace city for that king, he took his leave of the king and suddenly vanished, returning to the heavens.
At that time, King Mahāsudarśana, having seen that the palace city was entirely completed, immediately ordered the drum to be beaten to proclaim throughout the realm:
"King Mahāsudarśana, seven days from now, shall preach various teachings for all. Those who wish to hear them with joy may all assemble at the Dharma-preaching Hall."
At that time, when the brahmins, elders, householders, ministers, and common people heard this proclamation, they all assembled on that day.
At that time, the king immediately ascended the Dharma Hall and took his place upon the lion throne; all those who had gathered likewise sat upon thrones made of the four precious substances.
Thereupon, the king first expounded the ten wholesome dharmas for the assembly, and subsequently opened other gateways to the Dharma, continuing in this manner for twelve thousand years.
If any sentient beings in that land have ever heard the Dharma of that king, they will be reborn in the heavens at the end of their lives and shall not fall into the three miserable realms.
Ānanda! That king constantly brings such benefit to all sentient beings.
"Ānanda! At that time, King Mahāsudarśana, while in his private chamber, thought to himself:

'In my past lives, what karma did I perform, and what roots of goodness did I cultivate, such that I have been born into a noble family, possessing great majesty and virtue, with physical strength, vitality, and longevity unequaled by any man?'"
"It is precisely because I extensively practiced generosity, patience, and compassion in past lives that I have now obtained such a retribution;
I should now further cultivate superior progress."
He then engaged in reflection, and before long he attained the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna; he further cultivated the four immeasurable minds.
Ānanda! King Mahāsudarśana further instructed his queen and the court ladies to cultivate the four dhyānas.
