"At that time, there were eighty-four thousand white elephants in the Snowy Mountains who came every day and stood in formation."
Before the king’s palace, the king thought to himself:
"These white elephants constantly come to my presence; as they pass along the road, they trample upon living beings."
He then issued a command to the Minister of War, saying:

"From this day forward, there is no need for this elephant to come to me every day. Let it come but once every thousand years; forty-two thousand [years] will suffice, and there is no necessity for it to be exactly eighty-four thousand."

The King’s precious woman-jewel, named Shanxian (Sudhā), together with eighty-four thousand other ladies and court attendants, sat in meditation and contemplation within a quiet chamber for forty thousand years. They then said to one another:

"We have been sitting here in meditation and contemplation for forty thousand years without seeing the Great King; it is now appropriate that we go to pay our respects and inquire after his well-being."
Having spoken these words, they immediately followed one another to the place where the king was.
The other palace ladies entered and informed the king, saying:
"Sudhana has now arrived with eighty-four thousand women to pay his respects to Your Majesty."
When the king had heard this, he immediately went to the Dharma-preaching Hall and ascended the lion throne.
In a brief moment, Bhadrika and the others arrived, and the king called them forward.
Then, Suprabha and the others proceeded together to the king’s presence; they prostrated themselves at his feet and sat down in order, saying:

"We have been together in a quiet chamber, practicing meditation and contemplation for forty thousand years. It has been a long time since we last saw Your Majesty, so we have come to inquire after your welfare. We wish to say something; we pray that you will grant us leave to speak."
The king immediately replied,
"Excellent! Do as you wish."
Sudhana then addressed the King, saying:

"In this Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Uttarakuru, and Pūrvavideha—the four quarters—its inhabitants are exceedingly numerous, enjoying great wealth, happiness, and peace; they all practice the ten virtuous deeds, which is entirely due to the power of Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation."

In this Jambudvīpa, there are eighty-four thousand cities such as the city of Kauśāmbī; from all these cities, the kings, ministers, subjects, and brahmins have all come here, desiring to see the Great King.
Yet the King has sat in meditation for many years, so that those who come to pay court no longer see him, like a filial son who does not see his compassionate father.

Furthermore, throughout the four continents, people have not seen the Great King for a very long time as he travels; we only pray that Your Majesty will act appropriately for the occasion and care for your subjects.
"We women are weak and of no benefit to the kingdom; this is why we have practiced seated meditation for so long to our heart's content.

Your Majesty dwells in nobility, presiding over both the internal and external affairs of state, and there is not a single person among the populace who does not revere you. How could you possibly act as we women do?"
There are eighty-four thousand white elephants, chariots, and horses, each numbering eighty-four thousand; Your Majesty should mount them to travel and enjoy the sights.

In the past, Your Majesty constantly preached various Dharmas to all beings and bestowed upon them the ten wholesome paths of action, but lately, since you have been practicing seated meditation, these matters have been entirely neglected.
At that time, Subhadda admonished King Mahāsudassana with these various matters.
Having heard these words, King Mahāsudassana replied to him, saying:
"In the past and present, you have always exhorted me with virtuous matters; yet now, hearing your words, they seem utterly contrary to my former intent."
At that time, when Bhadra heard these instructions from the king, his heart was filled with distress; shedding tears, he thought to himself:

"The reason I previously remonstrated with the Great King was precisely because, according to my own view, I believed it to be the middle way; I did not expect that this would instead give rise to further transgression."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the king’s feet, and addressed the king, saying:
"Now, out of my own folly and ignorance of the correct principle, I have used this matter to offer remonstrance. I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me absolution for my repentance."
At that time, King Mahāsudarśana replied to Subhadda:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; even those joined together through affection must eventually part. Although these four continents are thus flourishing, I too shall soon abandon them."

In the past, I was an infant for eighty-four thousand years, a youth for eighty-four thousand years, a consecrated crown prince for eighty-four thousand years, and a consecrated king for eighty-four thousand years; only then did I become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

He ruled over the four continents with the seven treasures complete; for eighty-four thousand years he administered the affairs of the people, for eighty-four thousand years he expounded the various Dharmas to all the people, and for eighty-four thousand years he sat in meditation and contemplation.
From that time until now, fifty-eight thousand eight hundred years have passed; although such a lifespan is extended, it ultimately returns to exhaustion.
I am now old, and the time of my death is approaching. The ancient kings, with their noble status and pleasures, were no different from me; they too have passed away and returned to impermanence.
The city of Kauśāmbī and the other eighty-four thousand great cities have likewise perished; you should not develop attachment to this alone and allow your mind to remain long in negligence.

The reason I have now attained this exalted and supreme state is entirely due to the accumulation of various wholesome karmas in the past; it is now fitting that I should extensively plant various roots of goodness to create the causes for future lives, and for this reason, I have practiced seated meditation for many years.
At that time, when Bhadrika and the others heard these words of the king, their hearts were filled with great joy; they prostrated at the king’s feet and withdrew to their respective dwellings.

Not long after this, the king fell gravely ill and, knowing his life was coming to an end, he immediately installed the crown prince as king. He assembled the remaining ministers, brahmins, elders, and householders, and poured the waters of the four oceans over the prince’s head. When the ceremony was completed, the king passed away and was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
“Ānanda! Although King Mahāsudassana ruled over the four continents, his residence was only in Jambudvīpa.
Although he had eighty-four thousand great cities, the place where he dwelt was only Kusāvatī.”
Within the Snowy Mountains there are eighty-four thousand precious white elephants, yet the king rides no more than one.
Although there are eighty-four thousand fine horses, the king mounts no more than one.
Although there were eighty-four thousand chariots made of the seven treasures, the king constantly used no more than a single vehicle.
Although there were eighty-four thousand ladies, the one whom the king loved was but a single person.
There are eighty-four thousand jewel-adorned palaces, yet the king occupies no more than a single chamber.

As for his physical needs, mere sufficiency is enough; yet the king exerts his thoughts over the four quarters and entangles his mind in worldly affairs, laboring his spirit in vain without any benefit to himself.
"Ānanda! Was King Mahāsudassana anyone else?
It was I myself."

In the past, I attained this noble status; the kingdom and city where I resided were right here. In this very city, I served as a wheel-turning monarch countless times, bringing benefit and accomplishment to immeasurable sentient beings.

Now these devas fill the void; they were all formed through my teaching by means of various wholesome dharmas when I was formerly a king. Today they have come once more to this city to witness my parinirvāṇa, and I shall cause them to attain the fruit of parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda! For this reason, why do you say that this city of Kuśinagara is remote and narrow?
I am now determined to dwell in this city and attain parinirvāṇa.

When the Tathāgata spoke these words, hundreds of millions of nayutas of devas and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, free from dust and defilement; they then spoke to the Buddha with one voice, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the past, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you benefited us through all manner of wholesome dharmas; now, once again in this place, you establish us in the bliss of parinirvāṇa.
He immediately scattered named flowers and played celestial music, singing hymns of praise as an offering to the Tathāgata.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous!"
“World-Honored One!
In this city of Kuśinagara, such extraordinary events occurred in the past; I shall no longer harbor any thoughts of insignificance.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

“You may now enter the city of Kuśinagara and say to the Mallas: ‘Today, during the latter part of the night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Let all of you come to see me; if you have any doubts, ask whatever you wish without restraint. Do not let it be that at the time of my parinirvāṇa, you fail to meet me and later feel regret.’”

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda wept and was overcome with grief; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, composed his physical demeanor, and entered the city together with a certain bhikṣu.

At that time, in the city of Kuśinagara, the Mallas—men and women, old and young—began to assemble together to discuss the Tathāgata’s imminent parinirvāṇa; each of them desired to go to where the Buddha was.
Upon meeting Ānanda, he immediately asked:
"I have heard that the World-Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees; I am currently in the midst of conversation and wish to go to where the Buddha is."
Thereupon, Ānanda related in full the words commanded by the Tathāgata to the Mallas.
Having heard this, the Mallas wailed and lamented in grief; they fainted and fell to the ground, whispering softly among themselves: "Alas!..."
Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished; from this day forward, upon whom shall we rely?
We are like infants who have lost their compassionate mother. From now on, the realms of humans and devas will diminish, while the three evil destinies will daily increase and flourish.
They said to Ānanda,
"We and our retinues now wish to follow you to the place where the Buddha is.
At that time, Ānanda returned and informed the Buddha, conveying the World-Honored One’s words as he entered the city to announce them.
Among the multitude of Mallas, there were none who were not struck with awe, weeping and sobbing; they all came forward to behold and honor the World-Honored One.
All the Mallas, men and women, great and small, followed one another along the road, their tears flowing as they wailed.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing that the number of Malla warriors was exceedingly great, thought to himself:
"If each person in this multitude were to pay homage to the Buddha one by one, there would be no end to it."
"I shall now cause every household to pay homage at once.
When the multitude of Mallas had arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, Ānanda immediately addressed them all:
"Since the assembly that has come here is so numerous, if each person were to pay homage to the Buddha individually, you would not be able to finish in time."
"Now you may all pay homage to the Buddha at once, house by house.
The Mallas, having received this command, immediately paid homage to the Buddha, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray, World-Honored One!"
May I abide for one kalpa!
Or even less than a kalpa, I shall not enter parinirvāṇa, so as to benefit all devas and humans; for now, these sentient beings lack the eye of wisdom.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will provide guidance.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Malla, saying:
"You should not now make this request of me. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; the union of those bound by affection must inevitably end in separation."
"Even if I were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, this assembly would still eventually perish.
You should simply remember, uphold, recite, and contemplate the Dharma I have taught without forgetting it; in this way, it will not differ from my being present in the world."
When the Mallas heard these words of the Buddha, their request having been denied, they were filled with sorrow and distress; weeping and lamenting in grief, they remained silent.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist ascetic in the city of Kuśinagara who was one hundred and twenty years old, named Subhadra. He was intelligent and possessed great wisdom; he had recited the four Vedas and was thoroughly proficient in all scriptures and treatises, being revered by all people.
Upon hearing that the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the Śāla grove, he thought to himself:

"In all my books and treatises, it is said that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is extremely rare to encounter, occurring only once in a great while, like the blooming of the udumbara flower."
"He is currently staying in the Śāla grove; I have some doubts and shall go there to inquire. If Gautama can resolve my doubts, then he has truly attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Buddha was. Meeting Ānanda outside the grove, he said to him:

"In my books and treatises it is said that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; he appears only once in many hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, like the udumbara flower which cannot be seen even by counting. While he dwells in the world to teach and transform beings, I have never before seen him. Now I hear that he is in this Śāla grove about to enter parinirvāṇa. I have some doubts and wish to go and ask him about them."
"You should report to the World-Honored One on my behalf, saying: 'I now wish to have an audience with him.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard these words, thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One’s four elements are currently out of harmony; he has been receiving visitors for a long time, and his condition has already worsened."
"If we were to encounter these non-Buddhists again, there would surely be debate, which might lead to further harm and distress.
He then replied, saying:

"The World-Honored One’s four elements are currently out of harmony; he is lying down in the forest, suffering greatly from physical pain. You need not see the Tathāgata now; do not create an obstacle at the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa."
Subhadra made this request three times, and Ānanda likewise replied three times.

At that moment, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine ear, heard Subhadra’s voice as he requested of Ānanda; furthermore, observing that Subhadra’s faculties were such that he was ready to be delivered, he addressed Ānanda in a Brahma-voice:
"Do not alone create an obstacle for my final disciple. Allow Subhadra to come forward; I wish to see him."
"This man is upright, wise, and quick to understand; he has come seeking advancement and desiring to resolve his doubts and difficulties, not to engage in debate over victory or defeat.
Thereupon, Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, said to Subhadra:
"The World-Honored One has now commanded that you be granted audience."
When Subhadra heard that the Buddha had granted him permission to approach, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has certainly attained all-knowledge."
They then approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings with one another, and sat to one side. Addressing the Buddha, they said:
“Gautama, we wish to ask a question; we pray that you will grant us leave to do so.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Subhadra, ask whatever you wish. Subhadra then asked the Buddha:

“In this world today, there are the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the six heretical teachers—Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. Each of them claims for himself, ‘I am omniscient,’ and they declare that those who study under others hold wrong views.”
To claim that one's own practice is the path to liberation while asserting that the practices of others are the cause of birth and death,
and thus to engage in mutual criticism and condemnation— how can the truth or falsehood of such claims be known?
"Which teacher should be entitled to the title of 'śramaṇa'?
Which teacher is definitively the cause of liberation?
At that time, the Tathāgata replied to him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Subhadra!
You have been able to ask me about such a matter.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall speak for you. Subhadda!

If, among all phenomena, one does not perceive the existence of the Eightfold Noble Path, you should know that there is no such thing as a śramaṇa, nor a second, third, or fourth; they do not exist at all.
Since there is no śramaṇa, there is also no liberation;
since there is no liberation, there is no all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Subhadra!
If, among all phenomena, there exists the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path, one should know that there must necessarily exist the names of the four types of śramaṇas;
where there are the names of śramaṇas, there is liberation;
and since there is liberation, there is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhadra! Only within my Dharma is there the Eightfold Noble Path and the four designations of śramaṇas; this is the path of liberation and the knowledge of all modes.
Among those various non-Buddhists, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, their teachings lack the Eightfold Noble Path and the designation of "śramaṇa"; they do not constitute liberation or omniscience.
If one says that [a self] exists, you should know that it is necessarily a false and deceptive statement. Subhadra!

When any sentient being hears what I have taught, receives it with faith, and reflects upon it, you should know that such a person will certainly not have heard in vain, but will surely attain liberation.

Subhadra! When I was still in the royal palace before my renunciation, the entire world was deluded and intoxicated by the six teachers; at that time, no one could be seen who possessed the true reality of a śramaṇa.

Subhadra! At the age of twenty-nine, I left the household life to study the Way; at thirty-six, beneath the Bodhi tree, I contemplated the ultimate source and depth of the Eightfold Noble Path, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and realized all-knowledge (sarvajñā).

He immediately went to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of the rishis, and for the sake of the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths; they thereby attained the fruit of the Path.
At that time, the title "śramaṇa" first came into being, appearing in the world to bring benefit and welfare to sentient beings. Subhadra!
You should know that my Dharma can lead to liberation, and that the Tathāgata truly possesses all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).

At that time, Subhadra, having heard the Tathāgata teach the Eightfold Noble Path, felt great joy; his hair stood on end throughout his body, and filled with thirsty longing to hear the meaning of the Eightfold Noble Path, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One [would explain it to me]!"
"Please analyze for me the meaning of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately analyzed and explained it to him in detail.

Having heard the Buddha’s exposition on the meaning of the Noble Eightfold Path, Subhadra’s mind became clear and bright; he attained sudden and great awakening, and regarding all phenomena, he was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to go forth in the Buddha-dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One called out to him: "Welcome!"
"Monk! At these words, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One further expounded the Four Noble Truths for him at length; he immediately attained the destruction of the outflows and became an arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now know that at the site of enlightenment, I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
When he first preached the Dharma, he delivered the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Today, staying within the Śāla grove as he approaches parinirvāṇa, he preaches the Dharma for the last time and delivers Subhadra.
Among the devas and humans, there are none who should hear my preaching of the Dharma again in order to attain deliverance;
yet those with roots of goodness who ought to attain liberation shall all become my disciples in the future, instructing one another in succession.
Ānanda! Although Subhadra was a follower of external paths, his roots of goodness were such that they were ready to ripen; only a Tathāgata is able to discern and know this.
After my parinirvāṇa, if there are non-Buddhists who wish to seek ordination within my Dharma, you should not grant them permission immediately.

First, have them recite and study the scriptures for four months, and observe whether their disposition is false or sincere. Only when you see that their conduct is upright and gentle, and that they possess a genuine and profound aspiration for my Dharma, may you then allow them to go forth.
Ānanda! The reason for this is that you and others possess limited wisdom and are unable to discern the faculties of sentient beings; therefore, I have had you observe them first.
At that time, Subhadra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Previously, I wished to seek ordination.
World-Honored One, if you would require me first to recite and chant the scriptures within the Buddha-dharma for forty years before permitting my ordination, I am capable of doing so!"
"How much more so in the fourth month?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying: "So it is, so it is!"
"Subhadra! I observe your intention;
you have looked upon my Dharma with earnest longing and aspiration. That you now speak these words is no empty pretense.
At that time, Subhadra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I cannot bear to see the Honored One among gods and humans enter parinirvāṇa; today, I wish to enter parinirvāṇa before the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Excellent."
Then, at that time, Subhadra entered the fire-element samādhi in the presence of the Buddha and attained parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do not see my entry into parinirvāṇa and conclude that the True Dharma has here come to an eternal end."
Why is this? Because in the past, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I established the precepts of the Prātimokṣa and taught various other sublime Dharmas; these are indeed your Great Teacher.
"It shall be no different from when I am in the world. Ānanda!

After my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus shall each follow their proper order, showing mutual respect according to seniority; they must not address one another by family name, but shall all address one another by their given names."
Examine one another so that no one among the assembly violates the major precepts; you should not seek out the minor faults of others.
The bhikṣu Chandaka should be given a heavy punishment.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What heavy punishment shall be imposed?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! As for those who have been given heavy punishment, let no bhikṣu whatsoever speak with them.
Thereupon, Ānanda followed these instructions and carried them out.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you now have any doubts or difficulties, ask whatever you wish. Do not, after my parinirvāṇa, give rise to regret, saying:
'The Tathāgata was recently in the Śāla grove, yet at that time I did not go to consult him for a resolution, resulting in my mind being hindered today.'"
"Although my body is currently afflicted by illness, I am still able to explain away your doubts and delusions for you.
If you wish to uphold the True Dharma after my parinirvāṇa to benefit devas and humans, you should come quickly now to resolve your uncertainties."
The World-Honored One repeated this exhortation three times, yet the bhikṣus remained silent, with none seeking a resolution for their doubts.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!"
"Though he has thus instructed them three times, there is no one in this assembly who harbors any doubt.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Ānanda! Among this assembly now, there are five hundred bhikṣus who have not yet attained the Path; after my parinirvāṇa, in a future age, they shall attain the exhaustion of outflows.
"You, too, should be counted among them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you see any transgression or offense committed by my body, speech, or mind, you should speak to me."
At that time, when the bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, they wept in distress and said to the Buddha:
"How could the Tathāgata possibly have even the slightest transgression of body, speech, or mind?"
Thereupon the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; They are of the nature of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, Cessation is bliss."
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely impermanent.”
Although I now possess a body of vajra, I am likewise not exempt from being carried away by impermanence.
Within the cycle of birth and death, there is nothing more terrifying; you all should diligently practice with vigor and swiftly seek to escape this fiery pit of saṃsāra.
"This, then, is my final instruction.
The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived.
At that time, when the bhikṣus and the other devas and humans heard these words of the Buddha, they wailed and wept with grief, fainting and falling prostrate upon the ground.
The Tathāgata then addressed them all, saying:
"You should not give rise to such grief and affliction; the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely like this.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata entered the first dhyāna.
Emerging from the first dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the sphere of infinite space.
Emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Emerging from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of nothingness.
Emerging from the sphere of nothingness, he entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the meditative absorption of cessation.
At that time, having seen the Tathāgata thus serene and silent, his body and limbs no longer moving, Ānanda immediately shed tears and spoke these words:
“The World-Honored One has now entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Anuruddha said to Ānanda, “The Tathāgata has not yet entered parinirvāṇa;
the reason his body remains so serene and motionless is precisely because he has entered the samādhi of cessation.”

At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), returned once more to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), and proceeded through the stages down to entering the first dhyāna.
Emerging again from the first dhyāna, he entered the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, he entered the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he entered the fourth dhyāna, and in that very state, he entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Anuruddha said to Ānanda:
"The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa in the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
Thereupon, having heard these words from Anuruddha, Ānanda and the fourfold assembly wailed and sobbed with grief; they fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground.
Among them, some raised their hands, struck their heads, beat their breasts, and cried out loudly, saying to one another:
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished; how swift was it!
From this day forward, who shall be the guide for all sentient beings?"
"The humans and devas are now diminishing, while those in the evil realms increase day by day.
At that time, the gods, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings in the void wept profusely like a torrential rain, saying to one another:
"From this day forward, to whom shall we turn for refuge?"
It is like an infant who has lost its compassionate mother;
the paths to the three evil realms open wider by the day, while the gate of liberation stands as a massive, heavily barred door.
All sentient beings are thus submerged and sinking in the ocean of suffering.
It is like a sick person far removed from a skilled physician, or like a blind man who has lost his guide.
Since we have departed from the Unsurpassed Dharma King, the thieves of affliction daily see their encroachment.
Having uttered these words, he fainted in grief and agitation, unable to restrain himself.
At that time, the multitude of Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara were all brave and strong, like fragrant elephants.
Having seen the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa, his countenance was haggard and his spirit withered, as if he had recently risen from illness.

At that time, the great earth shook violently, the celestial drums resounded of their own accord, the waves of the four great oceans surged and overturned, and Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, naturally tilted and swayed. Furious winds arose, felling the trees and shrubs until they were shattered and withered, appearing utterly strange and extraordinary compared to the usual state of things.
At that time, the Great Brahma King spoke these verses:
"In the past and the future, And likewise in the present,
There is not a single sentient being Who does not succumb to impermanence."
The Tathāgata, honored among gods and humans, with a vajra-body as firm and solid, cannot escape impermanence; how much less so for other beings?
All sentient beings cherish and protect their own bodies.
Though one perfumes the remains with incense and flowers, one does not realize they shall perish.
The Tathāgata’s golden body, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, must likewise be relinquished; he should enter parinirvāṇa.
"Having forever severed all afflictions and attained the knowledge of all modes,
even such a one cannot escape [death], let alone those burdened by other fetters.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke this verse:
“The nature of all conditioned phenomena is truly that of arising and ceasing;
even the Most Honored One among bipeds shall likewise return to extinction.
The blazing fires of the three poisons constantly burn all sentient beings.”
"If there were no great cloud of compassion, who could rain down [to extinguish it]?
At that time, Anuruddha spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata this day, with all his faculties unmoving..."
The mind comprehends all phenomena and abandons this body;
Tranquil and free from discursive thought, it is likewise devoid of all sensation.
Just as a lamp’s light is extinguished when its oil is spent, So too is the extinction of the Tathāgata.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
"The great earth suddenly quakes, Fierce winds rise up from all four directions;
The waters of the ocean surge and overturn, And Mount Sumeru, the mountain of jewels, trembles."
The hearts of gods and men were filled with grief; they wept with tears like falling rain.
All were seized by great terror, as if possessed by non-humans.
Because of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such things occurred.

At that time, among the assembly were bhikṣus who had not yet attained the Way, as well as humans and devas; having seen that the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa, their hearts were filled with anguish, and they rolled upon the ground.
Those who had already attained the Way deeply lamented the suffering of impermanence in the world, wailing and weeping so uncontrollably that they could not restrain themselves.
At that time, Āniruddha addressed the bhikṣus and the devas:

"You should not give rise to great sorrow and distress; the Tathāgata has already explained to you previously that the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are exactly like this."
"Why do you still weep out of grief?
At that time, Ānanda addressed the assembly gathered from all directions:
"The Tathāgata has now entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, when the multitude heard Ānanda’s words, they wailed and wept with grief, fainting in their distress; then, in low voices, they said to Ānanda:
"This assembly of people is now extremely crowded, filling the space of thirty-two *yojanas*."
We only pray, Venerable One, that each of us may take turns coming forward to behold the Tathāgata in person, so that we may finally gaze upon him, pay homage, and make offerings.

The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter; he appears only once in a great while, like the udumbara flower. Now that he is personally present here at his parinirvāṇa, we pray that you will surely have compassion for us and allow us to see him.
At that time, Ānanda, hearing the words of the multitude, thought to himself:

"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare to encounter, and making an offering at the very end is likewise most difficult. Whom shall I now cause to be the first to make an offering to the Buddha?"
Now it is appropriate that the bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās be permitted to come forward first to make offerings to the Buddha’s body.
Why is this? These women are weak;
in the past, when they came, they were not necessarily able to reach the place where the Tathāgata was. For this reason, they ought to go first.
Having formed this thought, he immediately proclaimed everywhere:
"All bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās, listen! Come before the body of the Tathāgata."
The bhikṣuṇīs and immeasurable upāsikās together proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Having seen that the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa, they wept and lamented in distress; they circumambulated him, prostrated, and made various kinds of offerings.
At that time, there was a poor female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who was one hundred years old.

Seeing the various Brahmins, as well as Kṣatriyas, elders, householders, Mallas, their wives and daughters, and people of all ages—both young and old—all making offerings of various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers, she lamented her own poverty and isolation from this aspiration. She thought to herself:

"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; furthermore, to make an offering at the very end of his life is even more difficult. Yet now, being utterly destitute, I have no means to manifest my devotion."

Having formed this thought, his grief and anguish redoubled; prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet, he was overwhelmed with great distress, his tears flowing copiously so as to soil the Tathāgata’s feet:
“May I, in all future births, always be able to behold the Buddha.”
When the bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās had finished making their offerings, they returned to their respective places.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed all the other people, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās have completed their offerings; you may now come forward and make offerings in succession."

Then, the multitude of people arrived one after another at the place where the Buddha’s body lay; having seen that the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa, they wailed and rolled on the ground, their hearts filled with great sorrow and distress, as they made offerings with various ritual implements.
At that time, the multitude of Mallas all gathered together and said to one another:
"How shall we now perform the cremation of the Tathāgata’s body?"
"When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, there ought to have been a final injunction.
They then went together and asked Ānanda, "We now wish to perform the cremation of the Tathāgata’s body; what is the proper procedure for this?"
"When the World-Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa, he will surely leave behind instructions; we only pray that you will inform us.
At that time, Ānanda said to the Mallas:
"The Tathāgata’s final decree regarding the method of cremation is that it shall be no different from that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Ānanda then recounted in detail the matters the Buddha had previously commanded.
Upon hearing Ānanda’s words, all the Mallas together prepared the requisites for the cremation.
First, they constructed a precious carriage, exquisitely carved and magnificently adorned; they placed the body of the Tathāgata upon the carriage, burning incense and scattering flowers.
They performed various kinds of music and sang hymns of praise.
Amidst the music, he preached the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
At that time, the Mallas addressed Ānanda, saying:

"Now that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, this final opportunity for making offerings is extremely rare to encounter. We pray that you allow us to preserve the body of the Tathāgata so that we may offer worship as we please for seven days and seven nights, thereby allowing all devas and humans to attain peace for a long night."
Ānanda immediately relayed the Malla’s words to Anuruddha, and Anuruddha replied to Ānanda, saying:
“Excellent! Do as you wish.”
Ānanda then addressed the Mallas:
"Please permit me to retain the Buddha’s body for seven days and seven nights so that you may make offerings as you wish.
When the Mallas heard Ānanda’s words, their hearts were filled with great compassion and joy; they immediately made various offerings within the grove, and this continued for a full seven days.

At that time, the Mallas wrapped the Tathāgata’s body with new, pure cotton and fine silk cloth, and then placed it within a golden coffin. Inside the golden coffin, they scattered *gośīrṣa* sandalwood, fragrant powders, and various exquisite flowers. They then placed the golden coffin inside a silver coffin, the silver coffin inside a copper coffin, and the copper coffin inside an iron coffin. Finally, they placed the iron coffin upon a jeweled carriage and performed various musical performances, singing hymns and offering praises.

The devas in the sky scattered mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, and played various celestial music as offerings; thereafter, they successively lowered the coffin lids.
At that time, the Mallas said to one another:

"The seven-day period has now come to an end; we ought to carry the Tathāgata’s coffin around the city so that all the people may offer worship as they please, and thereafter proceed to cremate him south of the city."

Having spoken these words, they immediately set out to carry the Tathāgata’s coffin together; yet, though they exerted all their physical strength, they were unable to lift it, each of them being struck with wonder and not knowing the reason why.
They then questioned Anuruddha, saying:
"We, all these people, wish to carry the Buddha’s coffin around the city and return to the southern gate to perform the cremation offering;
yet, though we exhaust our physical strength, we are unable to lift it. We do not know what kind of omen this is."
"I only pray that the Venerable One will explain this to me.
At that time, Anuruddha said to the multitude:
"The reason for this is that the devas of the void desire the Buddha’s coffin to circumambulate the city."
Entering the city through the northern gate, one should listen to the various offerings made by the devas and humans.
Thereafter, one should exit through the eastern gate and proceed to the Ratnacūḍa Caitya to perform the cremation.
When those Mallas had heard these words, they said to one another, "The will of the devas is thus; we ought to comply.

They immediately carried the Buddha’s coffin around the city once, entering through the northern gate and halting in the center of the city, where they permitted the devas and humans to make offerings as they pleased, performing exquisite music, burning incense, scattering flowers, and singing hymns of praise.
The devas in the sky rained down māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, while playing celestial music and making various kinds of offerings.
Having completed the offerings, he immediately departed through the eastern gate of the city and proceeded to the site of the Ratnacaitya.

Upon arriving there, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the eight classes of beings—gods and nāgas—were so overcome with grief that they could not restrain themselves; they then gathered together ox-head sandalwood and various other incenses.

Furthermore, upon the funeral pyre, they spread fine silk and cotton cloth, and draped a great jeweled canopy over it. They lifted the precious coffin and circumambulated the fragrant pyre seven times, burning incense, scattering flowers, and performing various musical performances. Then, placing the precious coffin upon the pyre, they took exquisite scented oil and poured it all over it.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, together with all the devas and humans, were filled with such longing and distress that they could not restrain themselves; they immediately attempted to set it ablaze from below.
Yet the fire refused to ignite even after they tried a second and a third time, and still it would not burn.
At that time, the multitude did not know the reason for this and immediately asked Āniruddha:
"Three incense pyres have been prepared; why do they not burn?"
Anuruddha said:

"The reason for this is that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā when he heard that the Tathāgata wished to enter parinirvāṇa; he has come from that country with five hundred bhikṣus, desiring to see the World-Honored One."
"For this reason, the Tathāgata did not allow the fire to ignite.
At that time, when the great assembly heard these words, they sighed deeply in wonder at such a marvel.

At that moment, Mahākāśyapa was in the country of Daṇḍakīśvara; hearing from afar that the Tathāgata was in Kuśinagara and intended to enter parinirvāṇa, his heart was filled with profound grief and longing. He set out along the road with five hundred bhikṣus.
Not far from the city, his body being exhausted by fatigue, he sat beneath a tree with the bhikṣus by the roadside.
Seeing a non-Buddhist practitioner holding a mandārava flower in his hand, Kāśyapa asked him:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied,
"I have come from the city of Kuśinagara.
Kāśyapa asked again:
"Do you know my teacher, the Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha? He replied immediately,
"I know him."
"Your Great Teacher has already entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the śāla grove at Kuśinagara; seven days have now passed since then.

At this very moment, he is about to be cremated at the Ratnacaitya, and because devas and humans are filling the space, competing with one another to make offerings, I obtained these celestial flowers there."

At that time, having heard these words, Kāśyapa wailed with a sobbing voice, and the assembly of bhikṣus fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground. Then, in low voices, they spoke to one another: "Alas!..."
"Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa comforted him:
"You should not undergo such suffering and distress; the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely like this.
Even the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cannot escape them—how much less can others attain liberation from them?"
"You should apply yourselves with diligence to seeking liberation from worldly suffering; you may now quickly rise and go before the Ratnacaitya to pay homage and gaze upon it.
At that time, there were other bhikṣus among the assembly who had left the household life late in their years, being foolish and lacking wisdom, who said to one another:
"When the Buddha was in the world, he forbade and rebuked us, not allowing us to act according to our own whims."
"Now that he has entered Parinirvāṇa, how joyful this is!

At that time, Kāśyapa and the bhikṣus proceeded toward the city of Kuśinagara and arrived at the site of the Ratnacaitya. There they saw the Tathāgata’s coffin upon the fragrant pyre; weeping with sorrow and shedding tears, they circumambulated it seven times and then ascended the pyre.
Arriving at the precious coffin, he stood at the feet of the Buddha, wailing and sobbing, and prostrated himself with his head and face touching the ground.
At that time, the Tathāgata extended his two feet from within the precious coffin; seeing this, Kāśyapa’s grief and alarm redoubled.
At that time, when the devas and humans beheld this extraordinary and rare event, there was none who did not sigh in admiration and feel a profound sense of longing and attachment.
Then, seeing a stain upon the Buddha’s foot, Kāśyapa turned his gaze back and asked Ānanda,
"By what cause does this mark exist upon the Tathāgata’s foot?"
Ānanda replied:
"When the Tathāgata was first about to enter parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly was gathered in great numbers. At that time, I thought to myself:
'If I were to have the entire multitude advance at once, the women, being frail and weak, might not be able to reach the front.'"
He then first permitted the bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās to go to the place where the Tathāgata was to pay him homage and make offerings.
At that time, there was a poor upāsikā who was one hundred years old.

Seeing the various brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, elders, householders, and the wives and daughters of the Mallas—both old and young, great and small—all making offerings of exquisite incense and flowers in various ways, he lamented his own poverty and lack of means to express his devotion. Having formed this thought, his grief and distress redoubled; he pressed against the Buddha’s feet, his heart filled with great anguish, and as his tears flowed incessantly, they defiled the Tathāgata’s feet.

At that time, having heard these words, Kāśyapa was filled with sorrow and resentment; he reproached Ānanda for failing to rebuke [the Buddha] and prevent this defilement. He then offered incense and flowers to the Buddha’s coffin, prostrating and praising him.
When all this was completed, the two feet spontaneously re-entered [the body], and Kāśyapa immediately descended back to the ground.
By the power of the Buddha, the fragrant pyre ignited spontaneously, with flames rising from all four sides; after seven days had passed, the precious coffin was completely consumed.
At that time, the devas rained down fire to extinguish [the flames], and the multitude of Mallas collected the śarīras.
As for the thousand layers of cotton cloth with which the Buddha’s body had been wrapped, the innermost layer and the outermost layer remained as they were, unburnt, still encasing the śarīras.
At that time, the devas in the void rained down various wonderful flowers and performed music, singing hymns of praise as an offering to the śarīra.
Then, the assembled multitude and the Mallas all individually prepared various kinds of offerings.

The multitude of Mallas then collected the relics in golden urns, placed them upon a precious carriage, burned incense and scattered flowers, performed various musical entertainments, and returned to enter the city.
He erected a great high tower and placed the śarīra within it, then strictly arrayed the fourfold army to guard and protect it.
He permitted only bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs to enter to pay homage and offer various kinds of worship.
The other kings, brahmins, elders, householders, and all the common people were not permitted to approach.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, heard that the Mallas had taken the Buddha’s relics and placed them upon a high tower, where they were guarded by a strict fourfold army. His heart was filled with great sorrow and distress, and he became enraged at the Mallas; he immediately dispatched a messenger to speak to them, saying:
"When the World-Honored One was in the world, he was also my teacher."

At the time of his parinirvāṇa, we regretted that we were not present to witness it. My clan and the World-Honored One are both of the Kṣatriya caste; why is it that you alone have collected the śarīras, placed them upon a high tower, and now station the fourfold army to guard and protect them, while not sharing them with others?
"You may then give me one portion; I wish to erect a magnificent stūpa within my kingdom and perform various offerings.
If you grant this permission, we shall maintain eternal friendly relations between our nations;
if you do not grant it, I shall raise an army to invade you."
The other seven kings, as well as the Licchavis of Vaiśālī and others, all sent messengers with identical requests.
At that time, the brahmins, elders, and householders also each dispatched envoys to address the Mallas, saying:
"The World-Honored One was also our teacher; we pray that you will have compassion for us and grant us a portion of the relics."

At that time, the envoys from the various kingdoms arrived at the place of the Mallas and fully conveyed the King’s intent. Having heard this, the Mallas felt deep resentment and replied to the envoys, saying:
"The Buddha came to our country and entered parinirvāṇa; therefore, the śarīra naturally belong to us."
If you wish to construct a stūpa within the borders of our kingdom to adorn and make offerings to it, this shall not be permitted.

However, once the stūpa is completed, you may come here as you please to offer worship and pay homage at your leisure. As for raising an army to march against us, the military forces of this kingdom are sufficient to match yours.
At that time, those envoys each returned to their own kingdoms and reported these matters to their respective kings.
Having heard this, the kings became even more filled with rage and resentment; they each arrayed the fourfold army and set out to wage war.
At that time, the Mallas also prepared their weapons of war to confront the approaching enemy.
Within the city of Kuśinagara, there was a brahmin named Tuḷuṇa, who was intelligent and possessed great wisdom, and who had deep faith in the Triple Gem.
He thought to himself:
"Those eight kings and the Licchavis possess great physical strength, and their armies are formidable.
Furthermore, these wrestlers are so valiant that they are difficult to withstand; were we to engage in combat, it would surely not be possible for both sides to survive."
He then spoke to the Mallas, saying:

"Although you are all valiant, resolute, and courageous, those eight kings are united in purpose and strength; their hosts have gathered like clouds and their military arrays are fierce and formidable. If you were to engage in battle, it would be impossible for both sides to survive; once the blades cross, there will surely be injury and death."

"While the Tathāgata was in the world, he taught people to practice loving-kindness; yet today, you have suddenly engaged in mutual slaughter. You should not begrudge the distribution of the relics; it is fitting that they be divided among the various kingdoms and the Licchavis, so that each may erect a stūpa within their own borders."
"This accords with the World-Honored One’s former instructions and will cause you all to universally obtain benefit and merit.
When the multitude of Mallas heard these words, their minds were awakened and they replied, saying:
"What you have said is indeed consistent with reason; we shall listen according to your words."
When that brahmin saw that the host of warriors had all removed their armor, he immediately left the city and said to the kings:
"For what purpose have you now raised armies for the sake of the Dharma?"

The kings replied, "For the sake of the Dharma, we have traveled far to seek the śarīra; yet we have been met with refusal and opposition, and they are unwilling to share them with us. For this reason, we have now raised armies and come together."
Then the brahmin spoke again to the king, saying:
"I have already mediated for you with the Mallas; they have all agreed to give you a portion of the relics. You may take the precious urn, and I shall divide it for you."
The eight kings were filled with joy and respectfully presented him with golden vases.
That brahmin accepted the golden vases and, carrying them back, divided the relics upon a high tower and bestowed them upon the eight kings.
At that time, the eight kings, having obtained the śarīras, leaped for joy and, carrying them upon their heads, returned to their respective kingdoms and each erected a stūpa.
That brahmin, from the Mallas, begged for the vessel that had held the śarīras and erected a stūpa of his own.
The Mallas took one portion of the remains and, at the site of the cremation, combined it with the remaining ashes and charcoal to erect a stūpa;
in this manner, they erected ten stūpas in total.
From the time the Tathāgata first intended to enter parinirvāṇa, through his actual parinirvāṇa and up until his cremation, the construction of various stūpas occurred;
such were the events. Subsequently, Kāśyapa, together with Ānanda and the bhikṣus, compiled the Tripiṭaka at Rājagṛha.
